#6224. The Best Places to Go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific in 2027

When it comes to the best places to go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific for 2027, there is a prevailing theme: Familiar destinations are finding new ways to surprise us. In Queensland, old pubs have become home to some of the hottest tables. Just take a look at Noosa’s restored 100-year-old Kin Kin, which has a new lease on life thanks to the arrival of Michelin-trained chef Oscar Holgado. And there’s much more where that came from. Across the country in the East Kimberley, this is the year to dine on native bush foods in the shadow of ancient boabs and red cliffs, and rest your head at the area’s stalwart bush lodges, two of which have just reopened after major renovations. Then there’s Tasmania’s east coast, which is always deserving of a long road trip—and now Tasmanian malt whisky is being made in an oyster hatchery, not far from where little penguins (the world’s smallest penguin species) return to shore after feeding at sea. Across the Tasman, Wellington’s new Michelin guide reminds us that even those stars can’t capture the effortless excellence of this area’s food and wine culture. Plan your visit around a culinary festival, several of which come to life in winter, and you’ll see what we mean. Meanwhile, in the Cook Islands at Highland Paradise on Rarotonga, descendants of the original Tinomana community guide visitors through a 600-year-old ancestral mountain settlement, sharing its history and traditions as they optimistically await UNESCO’s answer on recognition. On our below list of the best places to travel in Oceania for 2027, there is a trip for every type. —Chloe Sachdev

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: ancient cultural sites, eco-tourism, dazzling island landscapes

On the South Pacific, the 15 isles of Cook Islands are scattered across nearly 900,000 square miles.

The Cook Islands’ 15 isles stipple roughly 849,000 square miles of the South Pacific, but total less than 100 square miles of land. Most first trips center on a southern pair of islands: Rarotonga and Aitutaki. On the one-hour propeller flight between two, the entire country arrives in flashes: a volcanic ridge inside a white reef, miles of open Pacific, then a blue lagoon with motu gathered along its rim. Rarotonga’s 20-mile coast road threads between reef and pleated peaks, while Aitutaki is defined by its broad lagoon.

On the west side of the island Rarotonga, a narrow road climbs from the lagoon into Maungaroa Valley, where a canopy of multi-trunked mato trees covers the remains of a centuries-old settlement. Taken together, the surviving sites form a cultural landscape that will appear before UNESCO’s World Heritage Committee in 2027 as the Cook Islands’ first nomination. At Highland Paradise, a cultural site within the old settlement and managed by descendants of Chief Tinomana, the Tapu’ae Day Tour follows those paths past chiefly house sites and sacred ground as guides explain how the stonework organized life here.

On Aitutaki, customary stewardship extends well below the waterline. In 2025 three lagoon zones came under ra’ui, a traditional temporary closure that allows coral and fish populations to recover, with protections scheduled to rotate in 2027. Aitutaki Coral Restoration takes small groups beyond the usual motu-and-sandbar circuit to its underwater nursery and a planting site, where guests clean a dead coral base and secure a naturally broken fragment. Part of each tour fee supports the restoration work.

Tourism is growing alongside the conservation push. In March 2027 a new, locally owned hotel, Grand Resort, billing itself as the island’s first five-star hotel, is scheduled to open with 61 adults-only suites on Rarotonga’s west coast. The Destination Stewardship Plan 2026–2030, meanwhile, shifts the focus from mainly growing tourism to managing its impact with protections for culture and the environment with a greater share flowing to island communities. —Paul Jebara

Go for: red dirt, remote lodges, and wilderness on an epic scale

After a multimillion-dollar transformation, Bullo River Station will reopen in May 2027.

Bullo River Station guests will have the opportunity to watch the seasonal mustering of cattle.

It’s not just helicopter blades creating a hum in Australia’s East Kimberley. A wave of luxury investment is putting this remote frontier on the global-travel radar—without sanding down the wilderness that makes it so worth the journey.

After devastating cyclone damage, Berkeley River Lodge welcomes guests back to a revived 15-villa hideaway, accessible only by private air charter from Darwin. Individual decks overlook a croc-filled coastline, while open-air en suites allow galaxy gazing from the bathtub. Just across the border in the Northern Territory, Bullo River Station sits on the eastern fringe of the East Kimberley. Come May 2027, it will reopen after a multimillion-dollar transformation, pairing a new level of comfort with conservation across its 400,000 acres. The good news is that it remains a dusty working cattle station: Guests can watch seasonal musters, fish for barramundi in the river, or helicopter to watering holes for swims beneath waterfalls or to Aboriginal rock-art sites.

There is even more to come. Abercrombie & Kent, in conjunction with the Billingjul Aboriginal Corporation, is developing its first Australian property: an off-grid eco-retreat offering access to the UNESCO World Heritage–listed Purnululu National Park, which contains the Bungle Bungle Range, where countless tiger-striped domes rise from the earth like sculpted beehives. (Originally slated for 2027, the lodge has been delayed, with a new opening date yet to be announced.)

Connecting much of this wilderness is Kununurra, a proper Outback town on the banks of the Ord River and the main jumping-off point for the Bungle Bungles, Lake Argyle, and the wider East Kimberley. If your itinerary calls for a night in town before heading deeper into the region, don’t waste it: The surrounding Ord River irrigation area is a surprisingly fertile food bowl. The Gourmet Camp Oven Experience puts that produce to work over four courses, cooked by fire in a secret off-grid location outside town, with dinner served beneath the stars and swinging chandeliers illuminating ancient boabs. —Katrina Lodge

Go for: heritage buildings, creative energy, and a new wave of boutique stays

In Western Australia, Fremantle's distinct creative scene centers on new boutiques, galleries, and stays.

Poppy Lissiman’s High Street flagship shines among a cluster of indie boutiques and maker pop-ups.

In 1987 the America’s Cup turned an unvarnished Western Australia port town into a global stage overnight. Forty years on, Fremantle has forged an identity of its own. Just 12 miles southwest of central Perth, Freo, as it’s known to locals—and Walyalup, as it’s known to the Whadjuk Noongar people—is the big city’s grittier cousin and the epicenter of one of Australia’s most eclectic creative scenes. This is, after all, fertile ground for Aussie homegrown musicians from Bon Scott to Tame Impala and John Butler. Now, right here at the mouth of the Swan River, a new generation of tastemakers are transforming warehouse skeletons and limestone heritage façades into galleries, natural wine bars, and boutique stays.

The energy will hit fever pitch in November 2027 with the return of the Fremantle Biennale, which will bring immersive art into the city’s forgotten spaces (dates are yet to be announced, but the 2025 event stretched over two full weeks). It crowns a year-round festival calendar of street performances, exhibitions, and community celebrations steeped in Fremantle’s multicultural roots. On the fashion front, a revitalization of the central piazza—just down the road from Aussie cool girl Poppy Lissiman’s High Street flagship—is helping spotlight indie makers and pop-up retailers. Fremantle’s historic West End has welcomed several hotly anticipated bars from beloved names in Western Australia hospitality, beginning with much-loved merchant Wise Child Wine Store, which expanded its bottle shop in September 2026 to include a 50-seat wine bar. Around the corner, Cafe Music, from the team behind Northbridge institution Wines of While, earned cult status with teaser weekends of mini martinis and vinyl DJs ahead of its permanent 2027 opening. At the heritage-listed P&O Hotel, listening bar and restaurant Ode to Sirens occupies the ground floor, while bartenders at Reuben’s Supper Club have been shaking cocktails since October 2026.

The West End’s newest stay follows the same past-meets-present script. The 11-room Owston Hotel (March 2026), inside the former Roma Restaurant, is a modern locanda honoring the Italian families who settled here in the 1950s. Breakfast comes from Common Bakery downstairs; later, slip next door for a pour at Vin Populi. —Jessie Stoelwinder

Go for: new sailings, revived resorts, and a quadrennial sporting showcase

Traveling by ship to French Polynesia has never been more accessible, thanks to new yachts and cruises.

With 118 palm-studded islands and atolls scattered across retina-popping blue waters, French Polynesia hardly needs help making a case for itself. But 2027 brings new ways to explore this far-flung corner of the South Pacific—especially by ship.

The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection’s French Polynesia sailings debut in December 2026, with 149-suite Evrima cruising the mountainous Society Islands, where volcanic peaks meet reef-ringed lagoons. In February, Windstar adds a second ship to sail these waters year-round, with the newly refurbished Wind Star joining Star Breeze throughout the Society Islands and the low-lying Tuamotus, a scattering of coral atolls and luminous lagoons. In March 2027, Aranui Cruises will launch Aranoa, a 91-cabin hybrid freighter-passenger ship bound for the remote Austral Islands, the Tuamotus, and Pitcairn. Wild, mountainous, and little visited, the Australs offer a different face of French Polynesia from the one seen in postcards showing overwater bungalows.

Though there are plenty of those accommodations on stilts, if that’s what you’re after, a wave of arrivals on land and lagoon add to the momentum. On mountainous Moorea, Sofitel Kia Ora Moorea Beach Resort has emerged from a major renovation in 2026, with revamped public spaces and refreshed overwater bungalows. In October, Bora Bora’s legendary Bloody Mary’s returned with a new 53-key hotel on Povai Bay and its sandy-floored restaurant restored alongside it. In early 2027, ELYT Charter Tahiti sets sail as a four-bedroom floating villa for private adventures around Bora Bora.

But 2027’s biggest arrival isn’t a hotel. In July the XVIII Pacific Games—the largest sporting event ever held in French Polynesia—will bring more than 4,500 athletes to Tahiti, Moorea, and Raiatea for 24 sports and more than 350 events. Among the sports is va’a, traditional outrigger canoe racing that is deeply embedded in Polynesian culture, alongside surfing, sailing, and open-water swimming. —Sarah Reid

Go for: Southland’s new cultural landmark, wild kiwi, and dark skies

Known in Māori as Rakiura, or “glowing skies,” Stewart Island is an International Dark Sky Sanctuary.

New Zealand doesn’t end at South Island. Farther down the map is Stewart Island, where the roads run out and the forest takes over. Rakiura, its Māori name, means “glowing skies”—fitting for an island that affords fiery sunsets, a visible Milky Way, and appearances of the aurora australis (southern lights) and is an International Dark Sky Sanctuary.

For many travelers heading to New Zealand’s deep south, the journey begins in Invercargill, where the Te Unua Museum of Southland will open in 2027, returning a major regional museum to the city for the first time since the Southland Museum and Art Gallery closed in 2018. Telling the stories of Murihiku Southland and its people, its collection includes rich holdings of Māori taoka, archaeology, photography, social history, and artifacts from the Subantarctic Islands.

Across Foveaux Strait, Stewart Island (Rakiura) comes into view. Oban, its only settlement, curls around horseshoe-shaped Halfmoon Bay. Wildlife vastly outnumbers humans here, where fewer than 500 people live. As many as 15,000 southern brown kiwi, or tokoeka, are thought to live on Stewart Island and, unusual for kiwi, can sometimes be spotted foraging in daylight. Just offshore, pest-free Ulva Island (Te Wharawhara) is a sanctuary for native birdlife like native kākā parrots and flightless weka birds.

Around 85% of the island is protected within Rakiura National Park, a wilderness of native forest, wetlands, dunes, and granite ranges. For a deeper look at its cultural history, take a boat from Oban to remote Oneke, or The Neck, an early Māori settlement and the tūrangawaewae—place of belonging—of Rakiura Māori. The three-hour guided experience begins with a whakatau, a traditional Māori welcome, and a visit to the Oneke whare (Māori meeting house) before guests follow coastal and native-bush trails as guides unpack the area’s Māori and European history, traditional plant use, and conservation. —Louise Goldsbury

Go for: lo-fi beach towns, long sweeps of sand, and a fast-evolving food scene

Elysium Noosa Resort joins Noosa's ever-improving food scene, serving an Italian-meets-Australian menu of local ingredients.

Elysium Noosa Resort is one of several new stays on Queensland’s low-rise, low-key Sunshine Coast.

An hour north of Brisbane, stretching along 62 miles of coastline and backed by rainforest-covered hills and volcanic peaks, Queensland’s Sunshine Coast is the antidote to both Brisbane’s big-city buzz and the Gold Coast’s five-star flex: lower-rise, lower-key, but home to an increasingly sophisticated run of ambitious openings that is raising its profile at home and abroad.

In Noosa the newly opened Elysium Noosa Resort has kicked lively Hastings Street up another notch. Cibaria Noosa trattoria, helmed by acclaimed Sydney chef Alessandro Pavoni, raids the Sunshine Coast food bowl for an Italian-meets-Australian menu of Queensland spanner crab risotto, Mooloolaba king prawns sharpened with finger lime, and locally sourced bistecca. Fifteen minutes south in Peregian Beach, two-hatted (”hats” are Australia’s equivalent of Michelin stars) restaurant Bask similarly puts local seafood, meat, and peak-season vegetables front and center.

Farther south, Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel, which opened in May 2026, has brought the lo-fi coastal town Mooloolaba its first internationally branded resort, with dazzling views and passionfruit-and-melon vodka cocktails at Sully’s Rooftop. On the waterfront at the Mooloolaba Spit, Fish House Steak & Grill jazzes up lobster rolls with a sunshiny yuzu emulsion. The region is serious about beer too: More than 20 independent brewhouses make the Sunshine Coast Australia’s craft-beer capital.

Inland, Casa Renoir, one of Australia’s chicest stays, will be completed in summer 2027 with six solar-powered villas. Limestone, olive trees, faded market finds, and private pools give the place the air of a Puglian masseria. That same connection to the land is shaping the hinterland’s food scene. Ēthos at Alsahwa Estate serves farm-to-table meals inside a barn on a 30-acre regenerative farm, while, in a plot twist for the 112-year-old Kin Kin Hotel, Michelin-trained chef Oscar Holgado, who has worked in the kitchens of Angela Hartnett’s Murano and Marcus Wareing’s The Berkeley, whips up a daily tasting menu—driven by whatever he’s plucked from the garden—in a converted barn called The Woodshed.

For all these developments, the Sunshine Coast hasn’t lost its low-key appeal; it has simply acquired better places to sleep, eat, and drink. Luckily, it is becoming considerably easier to reach with growing international connections and a $170 million expansion of Sunshine Coast Airport’s domestic terminal underway and due for completion in 2027. —Ute Junker

Go for: Rugby World Cup fever, landmark hotels, and a reinvigorated country escape

In 2027, the Men's Rugby World Cup returns to Australia for the first time since 2003, with the final Cup decider taking place in Sydney.

UNESCO-listed Greater Blue Mountains occupy more than a million acres of eucalyptus forest, sandstone escarpments, and deep-cut canyons.

Sydney has never struggled for attention, but 2027 is shaping up as a blockbuster year. The momentum began in November 2026, when Powerhouse Parramatta, the largest museum ever built in New South Wales, opened, bringing cultural heft to the city’s west. Also in November, Chanel staged its cruise 2026–2027 collection in Sydney. First shown in Biarritz, the fashion show found a natural second home in a city where salty hair, ocean swims, and year-round resort dressing are not just an aspiration but a way of life.

In 2027 sport takes over. The Men’s Rugby World Cup, expanded from 20 to 24 teams, returns to Australia for the first time since 2003, and Sydney lands the sharp end of the tournament. Over six weeks the city will host 13 matches, including major head-to-heads like Australia versus New Zealand, England versus Wales, two quarterfinals, both semifinals, and the bronze final, before 82,000 fans pack Stadium Australia for the final on November 13—the first rugby World Cup decider in Sydney in 24 years.

Australia’s first Waldorf Astoria opens in early 2027 on Circular Quay, with 220 rooms and serious architectural pedigree along with floor-to-ceiling views of the Opera House and Harbour Bridge. Kengo Kuma & Associates—behind Scotland’s V&A Dundee and Tokyo’s Olympic stadium—has designed a striking glass-fronted tower on the harbor. Inside, Melbourne-born Curtis Stone will lead the hotel’s culinary efforts, opening a bar and a restaurant—his first in Australia, in fact, after graduating from television chef to serious Los Angeles restaurateur with Maude and Gwen.

Two hours beyond Sydney, the UNESCO-listed Greater Blue Mountains stretch across over a million acres of eucalyptus forest, sandstone escarpments, and deep-cut canyons, promising the perfect side trip. Near Katoomba, the main hub for exploring the Blue Mountains, the historic Lilianfels hotel emerged from a multimillion-dollar overhaul in 2026 as Ardour Lilianfels Blue Mountains, its 89 renovated rooms and suites set on an 1889 country estate that is a well placed base for days on the trails. The bigger arrival comes in 2027, when Emirates’ long-shuttered Wolgan Valley returns from a $35 million-plus overhaul as the world’s first Ritz-Carlton Lodge, with 40 lodges scattered throughout a 7,000-acre conservation reserve roamed by kangaroos and wombats. —Chloe Sachdev

Long-known for its quiet beaches, Bicheno welcomes new names to the food and drink scene.

Dolphin Sands is a rural locality in the local government area of Glamorgan–Spring Bay in Tasmania

This area has long been home to one of Australia’s great road trips, a coastline drive linking Hobart with Launceston via Freycinet and the Bay of Fires. It’s a route of contrasts: the Tasman Sea on one side, forested hills on the other, past beaches and granite headlands, and a succession of fishing towns where boats still pull up with the day’s catch. Lately, though, there are more reasons to pull over.

Bicheno, two to three hours north of Hobart, is a case in point. The former fishing town turned low-key surf haunt remains better known for little penguins and deserted beaches than sceney restaurants, but a clutch of openings is evening the equation. At homegrown Waubs Harbour Distillery, award-winning whisky is made mere feet from the ocean in a converted oyster hatchery, with fireside tastings overlooking the Tasman Sea. Nearby, Le Gulch pours Tasmanian wines against pastel sunsets, while Parisian expat Tristan Punelle’s Le Coq, serving produce-led dishes by candlelight to a mix of both salty-haired locals and vacationers, is a humble ode to French cuisine. And after days spent surfing with dolphins and walking serene shorelines, Selkie Wellness restores balance at its beach-shack-housed massage studio and contrast therapy garden.

Farther south, beneath the pink-granite peaks of The Hazards, Saffire Freycinet enters a new chapter. In December 2026 the landmark wilderness lodge is unveiling The Saffire Jewel, an 8,600-square-foot, three-bedroom villa with a 59-foot-long infinity pool, a Jacuzzi, a private chef, and an excursion guide. Then, over Easter 2027, the Australian Three Peaks Race returns after a 14-year absence. The competition involves teams heading down Tasmania’s east coast in a nonstop combination of offshore sailing and mountain running. Spectators can watch the fleet depart from Beauty Point, catch the runners changing over at Coles Bay before tackling Mount Freycinet, or see the race finish in Hobart. —Alex Mitcheson

Go for: independent restaurants, wineries, and creative energy

In walkable harbor city Wellington, dining is defined by spots like Graze, Margot, The Ram, and Hillside.

For the best expression of New Zealand (Aotearoa) food, head to Wellington. Seriously. Michelin might have shone an international light on the country’s culinary scene in June 2026 but Wellington has been diligently perfecting its food culture long before the inspectors came to town.

This compact, walkable harbor city with a strong sense of community has been a go-to weekend escape for eating and drinking at some of the country’s best restaurants, bars, cafés, bakeries, and food festivals. A cohort of passionate chefs and owner-operators embody this sense of independent hospitality, taking advantage of local produce and the area’s abounding cultural diversity. In Wellington, you’ll find the kind of informal dining that the Michelin system often overlooks.

So how to tap in? At Graze in Kelburn, chef Max Gordy and sommelier Stina Persen serve a daily-changing menu built around New Zealand–grown produce and sustainably caught seafood. Over in Newtown chef Tom Adam and Juno Miers’s intimate Margot pairs seasonal cooking with an excellent drinks list. Elsewhere, The Ram recasts the Cuba Street pub as a serious food destination, while tiny vegetarian restaurant Hillside follows a low-waste philosophy grounded in local produce. Another to watch is award-winning Rita, which, in early 2027, will relaunch inside its century-old workers’ cottage as Super Rita, a deli and urban pantry showcasing local growers. The waterfront at Oriental Bay gets a new draw in early 2027, when The Pavilion opens its doors as an all-in-one food and wellness destination in a former 1930s bathing pavilion and band rotunda, with an all-day restaurant, a rooftop bar, and a bathhouse with hot pools, a cold plunge, a sauna, and treatments.

Bringing more of the creative energy Wellington is known for back to its Civic Square, City Gallery Wellington, a significant hub for contemporary art, reopened in October 2026 with a major exhibition by artist Cornelia Parker. Wellington’s city center continues to emerge butterfly-like from a long period of construction, and 2027 is a compelling time to visit, as several major civic buildings reopen to the public. Hot on the heels of the revitalized Te Matapihi ki te Ao Nui Central Library, the 120-year-old, heritage-listed Town Hall opens in February 2027 after more than a decade behind construction fencing, housing a new, world-class National Music Centre. From April 9–11, the restored venue will stage a new production of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Sunset Boulevard, starring Tony-nominated performer Keala Settle. —Johanna Thornton

Go for: major resort openings, reimagined experiences, and fresh ways to explore beyond the beach

The Whitsundays' reborn Le Méridien Lindeman Island Resort & Spa and Hook Island eco-lodge are much anticipated for 2027.

The Great Barrier Reef may be the Whitsundays’ headliner, with Whitehaven Beach its opening act. Now, though, there are fresh perspectives on the beloved archipelago. Explore Whitsunday Island beyond its coral reef by hiking the 20-mile, three-day Ngaro Track, which threads through subtropical forests and coastline. Along the way, you'll learn its stories through Traditional Ngaro Custodians. There’s also a new way to experience the Great Barrier Reef itself. Some 40 nautical miles offshore, at Hardy Reef on the outer Great Barrier Reef, Cruise Whitsundays has reimagined its floating Reefworld pontoon as an overnight-only experience: Sleep beneath the stars in one of 12 new glamping-style Reefbeds, or below the waterline in one of just two Reefsuites, Australia’s first underwater accommodations, offering floor-to-ceiling windows onto the reef and, if you’re lucky, a passing turtle. Next door the newly upgraded Heart Pontoon, a second floating platform, caters to day-trippers.

But the biggest news for the Whitsundays is the 2027 rebirth of two long-dormant island resorts. The 209-key Le Méridien Lindeman Island Resort & Spa—the brand’s first Australian resort—will bring an Explore Spa and a raft of water sports to Lindeman Island. More remarkable is the revival of Hook Island, which has been without a resort for more than a decade. The Whitsundays’ rugged second-largest island will get a low-impact eco-lodge with 39 cabins, forest pools, and wellness spaces, making the largely undeveloped landscape of lush rainforest, secluded bays, and color-popping coral reefs available to overnight guests once again.

On the mainland, don’t miss Sollos Estate, Australia’s first agave distillery, which has just opened north of Airlie Beach. The Whitsunday Skyway sightseeing cable car and a new five-star resort in development for Airlie add more reasons to visit this Sunshine State paradise. —Sarah Reid

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6223. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6222. American Plans Return to Israel, Partners With Israir

After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

The carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from New York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

Israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and New York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

American also said Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

“American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava said in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”

Israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. New York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

#6221. As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in New Zealand Took My Breath Away

After taking the 17-hour Air New Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand. I hopped around the North Island, relishing Auckland’s food scene, checking into the innovative Hotel Britomart, and visiting Wellington’s Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa. But when it came to the South Island, I realized the points of interest are far more spread out, with the massive Southern Alps to navigate through. The island has wide-open roads, but as an American conditioned to driving on the “wrong” side, I didn’t trust myself behind the wheel. So I turned to my favorite solution as a FOMO-fueled traveler who never wants to miss a highlight: scouring the GetYourGuide day-tour offerings to string together my ideal itinerary, a practice I’ve now participated in on all six continents.

I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown. And while New Zealand’s natural beauty and the genuine Kiwi kindness made every experience enjoyable, the highlight was my grand finale: the Milford Sound Business Class small-group tour starting in Queenstown from a local operator called RealNZ. The round-trip 12-hour excursion brings guests in a glass-roof Mercedes Sprinter for stops along the iconic Milford Sound Road, then aboard a Milford Sound cruise through the fjord known as Piopiotahi in the Indigenous Māori language, which some consider to be the eighth wonder of the world.

The wide-open views from the Sprinter van

I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed. Each of the 14 black leather seats had a gray lambswool blanket, a plush green pillow, and a bottled shot of Manuka ginger Vitamin C boost juice. As a ginger shot addict who’s constantly searching for the best natural pick-me-up around the world, it was love at first sight.

The long journey ahead—five hours each way—immediately shrank as our amicable guide provided context about where we were, explaining Milford Sound’s history, ecosystems, and Indigenous Māori connections. When all was quiet in the car, there was Starlink Wi-Fi to keep travelers entertained by their screens. After a quick refresher stop an hour in at the rural settlement of Garston, we reached the lakeside town of Te Anau, where one of its downtown shops served as our business class lounge.

Here, the coffee order I’d requested at the top of the day was already waiting in a covered reusable mug with my name on it, alongside a plate of pastries. It wasn’t long before we entered Fiordland National Park, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Te Wahipounam. I looked up through the translucent roof as foliage from both sides of the road enveloped our van, winding through the gentle curves.

Emerging through the Homer Tunnel, the writer stopped for this first glance of Milford Sound.

Soon, the narrow road opened up, and we made our first stop at Eglinton Valley, an expansive glacier-carved flat where expansive fields of golden tussock grass are broken only by striking triangular peaks. Not long after were the aptly named Mirror Lakes, where the Earl Mountains are reflected near-perfectly in the glassy, still water; and Falls Creek, a craggy cascade that unfolds into a teal pond. During our stop at Monkey Creek, we spotted a couple of kea, the world’s only alpine parrots known for their playful behavior. Next, we drove through the Homer Tunnel, traveling less than a mile through the solid rock of Darran Mountain. Fittingly, our guide changed the soundtrack to the Jurassic Park theme as we dramatically emerged into Milford Sound at last.

As we descended through the twisty road into the Cleddau Valley, there were gasp-worthy sights at every turn. One minute we were heading toward a daunting granite mountain wall and the next we were looking out to the waters of the sound in the distance. After a quick stop at a bridge to catch a glimpse of Fiordland's highest peak, Mount Tūtuko, in the distance, we arrived at Milford Sound Visitor Terminal to board the MV Sinbad.

A bridge across the Tūtoko River, which led to a view of Mount Tūtoko

The Cleddau Valley, with Milford Sound in the distance

That's when the premium service was cranked up a notch. After I was welcomed with a glass of local Cloudy Bay wine, I was led to my own bean-shaped wooden table with two cushy swivel chairs on one side and a couch on the other, set against expansive windows that stretched overhead for views of the peaks and falls.

A trio of dishes containing local ingredients, curated by chef Tom Hishon

Then came the five-course tasting menu. Already waiting was a seeded sourdough bun with whipped kelp butter, and it was followed by Fiordland wapiti (a local deer) bone broth soup. Next was a trio of artfully plated bite-sized dishes: paua (sea snail) with black garlic, a bite-sized fried ball made of titi (a local seabird), and roe from Mount Cook salmon. The penultimate dish was wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps plus smoked eel. It was all capped off with a “flat white”—an ice cream–topped dessert playing off the popular coffee drink.

Between dishes, the captain of the MV Sinbad talked us through the highlights of Milford Sound, steering us up close to its plentiful cascades, including Sutherland Falls (1,904 feet tall), Lady Bowen Falls (531 feet), and Stirling Falls (508 feet). When he noted that Niagara Falls is only about 180 feet tall, I thought I misheard and went over to ask. But despite the massiveness of Milford Sound, the falls exuded a calmness that overshadowed their height.

The area is home to bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins, and humpback whales, and we caught a glimpse of a New Zealand fur seal lounging at Seal Rock. Throughout the two-hour cruise, the peaks—some craggy and pointy, others smooth and sloping—were a reassuring constant.

Feeling rejuvenated thanks to both the power of Mother Nature’s beauty and the gourmet dining, we eventually returned to the van, where a generously sized bag of Marlborough Sea Salt Proper Crisps was waiting on my seat along with a Whittaker’s bar, New Zealand’s most famous chocolate. Of course, since it is business class, I also received a refreshing hand towel as I boarded.

As we began the journey back to Queenstown, I gazed upward, soaking in the view from the car’s glass roof, with a contented smile. A rest stop later, I was so relaxed that I drifted off into a deep sleep. The next thing I knew, we were back in the city. We had spent 10 hours out of the 12-hour trip inside the van, but I hardly realized it thanks to all the luxurious touches at every turn. In this case, the journey was absolutely part of the destination.

The Milford Sound Business Class tour launched in October 2025 as a joint operation between RealNZ and Altitude Tours. I originally saw the offering on GetYourGuide, my preferred tour booking platform for its flexible cancellation policies, but you can also book directly through the RealNZ website. The excursion starts at $383 per person for the business class tour, but a coach version is also available.

The tour I took transferred from Queenstown, but RealNZ also offers the trip from Te Anau, as well as a self-drive experience. There’s also the option to book travel back to Queensland via a 45-minute flight in a fixed-wing aircraft for an additional cost, though it’s weather-dependent. For those seeking deeper immersion, there’s also an overnight cruise through Milford Sound, with the choice of private cabins with en suite bathrooms or shared bunk-style compartments.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

It’s the end of an era at American Airlines.

This week, the carrier (officially) bid farewell to Flagship First international service.

We’ve been talking for years about American’s plans to retire its international-style first-class product.

The airline is replacing Flagship First with larger and more modern business-class cabins on its marquee planes — cabins that will feature its next-generation Flagship Suites.

But there’s at least a little nostalgia in bidding farewell to a cabin that, for many years, was billed as American’s most exclusive.

American was the last U.S. airline that claimed to offer a standalone, international first-class product.

Across the global airline industry, many carriers sunset long-haul first-class years ago, choosing to instead offer more — and improved — business-class seats, which take up less space and are considered more profitable.

For years, Delta Air Lines’ Delta One business-class suites have been its premier long-haul offering.

United Airlines bid farewell to international first class in 2018 when it pivoted to Polaris business class.

That left American’s Flagship First as a relic, of sorts, in the U.S. airline industry — and even on its own planes.

In recent years, you could only find the cabin on two fleet types American operated: its Boeing 777-300ER, which offered eight of the pods up front in their own dedicated cabin.

Plus, AA still (for now) offers Flagship First on its three-cabin Airbus A321T, which has been a fixture on lucrative coast-to-coast routes like New York to Los Angeles and San Francisco.

But soon, it will be a thing of the past on both planes.

American is retrofitting its larger 777s, ditching first-class in favor of 70 all-new Flagship Suites in business-class — along with the biggest premium economy cabin it’s ever offered.

Related: This is now American Airlines' most premium plane: Here's what it's like on board

On domestic routes, the A321T will actually keep flying with Flagship First through March 28.

But after that, AA will stop selling the Flagship First cabin on the A321T configuration, which is eventually going away as American flexes in its new A321XLR planes fully onto its top cross-country flights.

In a lot of ways, American ditching Flagship First is a positive (and arguably overdue) transition for flyers.

It’ll give passengers more lie-flat seats to pick from, whether they’re paying cash, using AAdvantage miles or using a systemwide upgrade.

Also — while those Flagship First seats were really spacious and comfortable, many would say that American's new business-class product is a major upgrade from what it previously offered in that cabin.

On some planes, that even includes extra-spacious Flagship Suites Preferred in the front and bulkhead rows of some planes, which offer a lot more space.

Value check: Is it worth buying up to American Airlines' new business-class Flagship Suite Preferred?

Beyond the aircraft, American also plans to still offer many of the same amenities for business-class that first-class passengers historically enjoyed.

For instance, its Flagship business-class tickets get access to its premium lounges. Passengers traveling in Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus on qualifying international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes will also be able to have a meal in its exclusive restaurant-style dining rooms in Dallas, Los Angeles and Miami.

The experience is available on a space-available basis.

So, in some ways, you could argue the end of Flagship First is more symbolic than anything.

But for some AA loyalists, it's still a little bittersweet.

TPG’s Clint Henderson is our resident Flagship First enthusiast, having flown the cabin on dozens of occasions.

"The service in first class wasn't particularly differentiated, but I still liked a few of the special touches," he said, pointing to the additional soup course and appetizer, along with a handful of elevated amenities.

He especially appreciated the “La-Z-Boy-style” seats at the front of American’s 777s, which could lie flat or swivel and turn into an “office in the sky.”

“While these cabins are definitely showing their age,” Henderson added, “I’m sad to see it go.”

While Flagship First is technically going away as an official cabin on international service, the seats themselves won't disappear overnight.

So far, American has only retrofitted one of its 20 Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the seats. That means a handful of jets with the old first-class seats will still be flying around well into 2027.

Going forward, the former Flagship First seats on those planes will be marketed as business-class. They won’t come with the full first-class service, but you’ll still get the elevated seat.

#6219. American’s Longtime Chief Operating Officer to Retire

American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.

Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

“He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

American will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A new reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

“For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

#6217. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6216. Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

#6215. The Right Tote Bag Is the Ultimate Travel Companion—These Are Our Editors’ Favorites

If you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option. From early morning flights to daily office commutes, or even a packed Saturday afternoon at the farmers market, our editors are always relying on their favorite tote. The best tote bags hold everything from our laptops, headphones, and water bottles to sleep masks and our most-used beauty products. Whether you reach for a structured leather version to pack your essential items in or an oversized, canvas carryall for a day at the park, the functions of the right tote are infinite.

Though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler. My favorite tote has been my everyday work bag for years, but it has also accompanied me on countless flights, weekend getaways, and last-minute happy hours. A reliable tote bag really can do it all. Keep reading to discover 15 of our editors' favorite tote bags and why we can’t live without them.

Coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager. Though I still cherish that tiny bag, my most used Coach item is my leather tote. For years, the Nina Tote bag has been my reliable sidekick. I’ve had it for so long that Coach no longer produces it. On the bright side, the Maggie Tote bag is almost identical to mine and is just as practical. I have put my bag through anything and everything over the years, and there is very little wear and tear. The leather is structured and durable, yet flexible enough to fit everything I need without toppling over. With plenty of interior pockets, my necessities all have a place, so I never have to go digging through the bottom of my bag to find the right lip gloss. Not only do I love traveling with this tote, but it’s also my everyday work bag and my go-to for almost every kind of activity.

I've never really had a work bag that I truly loved until I tried this one from Cuyana. What I appreciate about the System Tote are the additional organizational accessories that you can purchase to add a bit more structure to the interior. Aside from lugging it to and from the office each day, I use this tote as a personal item on the plane and brought it with me on a road trip to Acadia National Park, and have found it to be the ultimate travel companion. The built-in interior pocket is perfect for storing essentials you need to reach easily, like your passport, earbuds, or some petty cash, and since the bag can be snapped closed, you don't have to worry about anything flying out. —Jamie Spain, travel bookings editor

This bag is all about the pockets. No tote has ever kept me quite as organized as this one from MZ Wallace, a brand known for its signature quilted bags. It offers six interior pockets, five exterior pockets, and a detachable pouch, offering me a dedicated space for all of my essentials plus a whole lot more. I’m always impressed at how much this thing fits; an umbrella, my 13-inch laptop, a full change of clothes, and my lunch. The Medium Metro tote features ultra-soft shoulder straps, making it a go-to for commutes to the office. My favorite thing about this bag is how lightweight it feels even when full—it never digs into my shoulders or hurts my arms. More features that make this roomy tote a smart choice for travelers: a luggage sleeve, protective feet, and a detachable and adjustable crossbody strap. —Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

Monos’s Metro Tote has been with me longer than most New Yorkers are in relationships. I’ve had this faux-leather cutie for nearly five years now, and it’s traveled with me through new jobs, new apartments, and plenty of new adventures. I actually bring it to work with me every day—the laptop sleeve and spacious interior keep me organized on my way to and from the office. —Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor

I've received so many compliments on this gorgeous structured bag from Cuyana—it's been a great work bag, with plenty of space for my laptop, planner, Kindle, chargers, and other day-to-day essentials. I wasn't sure how well it would function as a personal item as there's not a zipper to fully close the bag, but on a flight to Aruba, I made use of the leather ties to keep items contained, and found it well-sized to slip under the seat in front of me, even with my toiletry bag and a sweatshirt stuffed inside. I'm also a big fan of the snap-to-close key leash, and the interior slips pockets and zipper pocket. —Madison Flager, commerce director

The bag is perfect in the way a red apple sitting on a teacher’s desk is perfect. It’s classic, without ornament, the kind of thing that expresses its utility in its design. It’s both ubiquitous and aspirational, stirring up images of a dreamy East Coast: a white-sand, Nantucket beach; a shabby, wood-planked boathouse on the coast of Maine; a Gothic-inspired Ivy League campus. I've used it as a carry-on item, a beach tote, and as a weekender. Simply having it out on display in your home has the power to imbue your space with a charming, outdoorsy vibe. —Jessica Sulima, commerce writer

Baggu’s Nylon shoulder bag is more durable than its canvas tote bags but equally as stylish. It’s slightly slouchy, slightly structured, and comes in the signature Baggu colors and patterns. The adjustable quilted shoulder strap allows for a crossbody fit, a must-have for me when I’m commuting into the office or walking longer distances (nobody needs their laptop sliding off their shoulder onto the sidewalk). The zip closure and interior pockets are handy for organizing miscellaneous goodies and preventing spillage. Plus, the lightweight material can easily be flattened to fit into my suitcase. I find myself continuously reaching for this multipurpose tote on my way to the gym, office, farmers market, and airport. —Hannah Towey, associate editor

Just when I think I’ve run out of room, I haven’t. The expandable bottom of this Calpak laptop tote adds an extra four inches, allowing me to add last-minute essentials or souvenirs mid-trip. Like all products in the brand’s Luka collection, it’s made of a lightweight, ultra-soft, puffy exterior that makes carrying its handle easy. The material is also easy to clean—simply wipe away dirt or spills without a worry. Inside, there’s a padded 15" laptop sleeve, multiple side pockets, and a zippered section to keep smaller items organized. Another feature I love: There’s a zippered pocket on the outside that keeps my phone or passport secure, while still being easy to access. It’s a great tote for commuters and thanks to its luggage trolley sleeve, an ideal carry-on bag for travelers. —M.K.

As a shopping writer who is constantly running between the office, press previews, catch ups with friends and, of course, the airport, I need a bag with space for all the day’s exploits and then some. July’s Juliette Soft Work Tote is my perfect do-it-all companion. It’s beautiful—I’ve received multiple compliments on this bag as I’ve been whizzing around with it, and the divided interior is really clever. There’s a 14" laptop sleeve to keep tech protected—all the more important when you’re headed on a flight— and there’s also a dedicated water bottle holder too. It has a wide bottom so your lunchbox can go inside flat, plus a key leash to stop the rummage for your house keys. Brushed gold hardware and a buttery-soft faux leather exterior mean it looks effortlessly chic at after-work drinks, and when I'm off to the airport, the removable trolley sleeve slides over my suitcase handle so I can breeze through the terminal. It is my favorite desk-to-departure tote bag. —Charley Ward, commerce writer, Condé Nast Traveller UK

My Strathberry Kite is my most-used travel accessory. Not only do I use it for day-to-day tasks, it comes with me on almost every trip (the exception being adventure travel), and most recently carried me through trips to Lisbon and Istanbul, where I spent weekends catching up with friends and sightseeing. It's an ideal size for a laptop, should you wish to take it, but fits in plenty of other necessary items, too (like flip-flops or ballet flats after hours of strolling through cobbled streets). I love the walnut color and the soft, supple leather. I'm sure this will be a favorite of mine for years to come. —Abigail Malbon, global audience development manager

When I first saw Parker Thatch offers its Jack Tote bag in this unique zebra and burgundy color combo, I knew it had to be mine. I never travel without animal print, and there was something about this colorway that felt perfectly understated yet maximalist. I found it online about a year ago, and it sold like hot cakes—and has been (devastatingly) sold out since. I received it as a sweet gift from my partner a few months ago, who had pre-ordered it to arrive right when it was back in stock. I've been using it as my go-to work bag ever since. It has an incredible amount of space and strength to carry all of my everyday essentials and then some—from my laptop and a book to makeup and toiletries. Because of its exterior fabric as hair-on cowhide, she just needs to be shielded from the rain a bit more than your average bag. If the design is calling your name on this bad boy, it’s well worth the splurge. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

I love anything Longchamp, and this gorgeous beach tote from the brand is my cherry on top of any vacation outfit. It’s large enough to hold a full day’s worth of goodies (sunscreen! sweatshirt! beach read!), but fits on the shoulder with ease. Plus, the toggle on the front keeps things contained in the most Longchamp-esque way. —H.C.

After passing the gauntlet of a last-minute trip to the British Virgin Islands, I always keep the Foldie Travel Bag on me, whether it’s riding in my backpack during my daily commute or stuffed into my suitcase on longer hauls. The front pocket easily held my thick reading list and two Moleskine classic notebooks; the full 40 liters of space in the main compartment (with the expansion unzipped) fit a week’s worth of clothes, chargers for four different devices, and another bag filled with toiletry bottles, plus room to spare for souvenirs. Another perk: the two inner pockets and wet pocket proved useful in sorting out the bag’s increasingly chaotic contents. The luggage sleeve was a relieving bonus that allowed me to transfer the hefty weight of my zealous packing to my suitcase. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations

I absolutely love this tote. Whether I’m wearing it to the office or while traveling, it fits everything I need. Plus, it comes with a separate removable pouch that I use even when I’m not wearing the bag. This slouchy bag is super durable and matches any outfit. —Pooja Nayyar, associate social media manager

Sentimentality may cloud my vision, for the tote in my possession belongs to my late grandmother. And when I tell you I was complimented frequently for it while in Italy, I mean I felt I needed to use the bag to beat back admirers waxing: “Wow, is Vera Bradley back?”; “Is it reversible?!”; “The textiles are so beautiful.” I often caught myself fantasizing about dumping it upside down to perform a “What’s in my bag” for nobody in particular—so capacious is the tote that I was needlessly carrying multiple novels within and rarely remembered to leave my toiletry kit on the hotel bathroom counter where it belonged. Handy pockets ringing the interior are just icing, and would have kept my passport safely inside had I ever been moved to act on the aforementioned dumping. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

#6214. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6212. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.
