#6197. Why All 3 Of Boeing's Most Modern Aircraft Have Drastically Different Wingtip Designs

Boeing's three most modern commercial aircraft, the Boeing 737 MAX, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and Boeing 777X, share a common objective when it comes to their wing designs: reducing aerodynamic drag and improving fuel efficiency. However, despite pursuing the same goal, all three aircraft feature noticeably different wingtip designs, ranging from distinctive split-tip winglets to swept-back extensions and even enormous folding wingtips.

The differences are not simply a matter of appearance or Boeing experimenting with alternative technologies. Instead, each design reflects a combination of aerodynamic performance, aircraft dimensions, and the practical limitations imposed by airports. Understanding why these aircraft have such different wingtips provides an interesting insight into the compromises involved in modern aircraft engineering.

An aircraft's wingtips play an important role in determining how efficiently it flies, particularly during cruise. As air moves around a wing, higher-pressure air beneath the wing attempts to move toward the lower-pressure region above it. This movement creates swirling vortices around the wingtips, which contribute to a phenomenon known as induced drag. The resulting resistance makes it harder for an aircraft to maintain speed and requires additional engine thrust.

Reducing induced drag is therefore a major consideration when manufacturers design new commercial aircraft. One of the most straightforward ways to achieve this is by increasing the wingspan, effectively distributing lift across a longer wing and reducing the strength of the vortices produced at its extremities. However, making wings longer introduces another challenge, since airports have strict limits on how much space aircraft can occupy.

The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) establishes aircraft size categories that help airports determine which aircraft can use particular gates, taxiways, and other infrastructure. These categories are largely determined by wingspan, meaning manufacturers cannot simply make every aircraft's wings as long as they would ideally like. An aircraft that exceeds the relevant dimensions could require different airport facilities, potentially limiting its operational flexibility.

Boeing's engineers must consequently balance aerodynamic efficiency against the practical requirements of commercial aviation. Different wingtip devices offer different ways to manage this compromise. Some extend the effective wing vertically, while others increase the actual wingspan or combine both approaches. The three aircraft demonstrate how these engineering decisions can produce substantially different solutions to essentially the same aerodynamic problem.

The Boeing 737 MAX features perhaps the most visually distinctive wingtip arrangement of the three aircraft. Its Advanced Technology winglets have two separate extensions, with one pointing upward and another extending downward. This split-tip configuration gives the aircraft a distinctive appearance while helping reduce induced drag without requiring a substantial increase in its overall wingspan.

The reason Boeing selected this particular arrangement becomes clearer when considering the aircraft's relationship with the 737 Next Generation family. The Boeing 737 MAX was developed to retain considerable operational commonality with its predecessors, allowing airlines to introduce the newer aircraft without requiring significant changes to their existing airport infrastructure. Keeping its wingspan within the ICAO Code C limit of 118 feet (36 meters) was therefore an important design consideration.

A conventional raked wingtip, such as the arrangement found on the Boeing 787, would have extended the 737 MAX's wings too far horizontally. This could have pushed the aircraft outside the dimensions associated with its existing airport category, creating complications for airlines operating it alongside older 737 variants. The split-tip design improved aerodynamic performance while keeping the aircraft within its required dimensional limits.

The winglets also incorporate carefully shaped surfaces designed to manage airflow and reduce aerodynamic losses. Rather than simply adding extensions to the existing wing, Boeing developed a more sophisticated arrangement intended to improve overall efficiency. This was particularly important for an aircraft that needed to deliver better fuel economy while retaining much of the operational flexibility that had made earlier 737 generations attractive to airlines.

The latest data from ch-aviation shows that Southwest Airlines is currently the world's largest operator of the Boeing 737 MAX, with a total of 300 in its fleet, followed by United Airlines with 243.

Boeing has achieved its first target for MAX deliveries, but is still working to reach the higher rate of 47 deliveries a month.

Unlike the 737 MAX, the Boeing 787 was developed as an entirely new aircraft family, giving Boeing considerably more freedom when designing its wings. Rather than adopting conventional vertical winglets, the manufacturer opted for long, swept-back raked wingtips that extend the wing horizontally. The result is a particularly elegant design that contributes to the 787's distinctive appearance.

The Boeing 787's wing design was developed with aerodynamic efficiency as a central priority, rather than being constrained by the dimensional requirements associated with an existing narrowbody aircraft family. Its larger wingspan allows the aircraft to benefit from the reduced induced drag associated with longer wings. Boeing was therefore able to pursue a solution that offered aerodynamic advantages without introducing conventional upward-pointing winglets.

Research from Boeing and NASA indicates that raked wingtips can reduce drag by approximately 5.5%, compared with improvements of around 3.5% to 4.5% for conventional winglets. Although the precise benefits depend on the aircraft and operating conditions, these figures help explain why Boeing selected this configuration for its widebody aircraft. The design also avoids some of the additional structural weight associated with separate winglet structures.

United Airlines is currently the world's largest operator of the Boeing 787, as outlined in the table below:

Another important characteristic of the Boeing 787's wings is their composite construction. Built primarily from advanced carbon-fiber-reinforced materials, they are designed to be long, relatively thin, and flexible. This flexibility allows the wings to respond to aerodynamic forces during flight, while their overall shape contributes to improved efficiency. Combined with the raked wingtips, the design helps the 787 achieve the aerodynamic performance required for long-distance commercial operations.

The Boeing 777X takes the concept of longer wings considerably further, featuring the largest wingspan of any commercial airliner currently designed for airline service. Its wings extend 235 feet (72 meters) when fully deployed. This substantial span helps reduce induced drag and supports the aircraft's objective of delivering improved fuel efficiency on long-haul routes.

However, the Boeing 777X faces a practical problem that the 787 does not encounter to the same extent. Its enormous wingspan would exceed the dimensions permitted within the ICAO Code E category used by many large commercial aircraft. This could make it difficult for the aircraft to operate at airports designed around the existing infrastructure used by conventional widebody aircraft, potentially restricting where airlines could deploy it.

Boeing's solution was to develop folding wingtips that allow the outer sections of the wings to rotate upward while the aircraft is on the ground. Once folded, the 777X's wingspan is reduced to just under 213 feet (65 m), bringing it within the dimensional requirements associated with Code E airport operations. Before take-off, the wingtips extend into their normal flight positions, restoring the aircraft's full aerodynamic configuration.

This arrangement is particularly interesting because it allows Boeing to avoid choosing between aerodynamic performance and airport compatibility. The aircraft can benefit from an exceptionally long wing during flight without requiring airports to accommodate its entire wingspan while parked or taxiing. The folding mechanism adds engineering complexity, but it provides a practical solution to a problem that would otherwise have required substantial compromises in wing design.

This innovative design feature has captured global attention.

The Boeing 777X is set to become the latest and largest member of the manufacturer's successful 777 family. Designed to offer improved efficiency, greater range, and increased passenger comfort, the aircraft will be available in three variants: the 777-8 and 777-9 passenger models, along with the 777-8F cargo aircraft. The Boeing 777-9 will be the first variant to enter service, offering airlines a high-capacity long-haul aircraft. The smaller 777-8 will provide greater range, while the freighter version targets the growing cargo market.

However, the program has experienced considerable delays. Originally expected to enter service in 2020, the Boeing 777X has faced certification challenges, flight-testing setbacks, and issues involving its new GE9X engines. As of November 2026, Boeing is targeting the first 777-9 delivery in 2027. The 777-8F is expected around two years later, while the passenger 777-8 is not anticipated before 2030. Despite the setbacks, the 777X remains an important part of Boeing's future long-haul aircraft plans.

Emirates is set to be the world's largest operator of the Boeing 777X, with a staggering 270 on order. The carriers with the largest firm orders for the passenger variants of the 777X (777-8 and 777-9) are outlined in the table below:

Although the three Boeing aircraft use different solutions, their wingtip designs are based on the same aerodynamic principles. All three aim to reduce induced drag, improve lift distribution, and lower the amount of energy required to maintain efficient flight. The differences emerge because each aircraft operates within a different set of dimensional and engineering constraints, rather than because Boeing has changed its overall approach to aerodynamic efficiency.

For the Boeing 737 MAX, airport compatibility was particularly important because the aircraft needed to retain the operational flexibility of the previous 737 generation. Its split-tip winglets provide aerodynamic improvements without substantially increasing its wingspan, making them a practical solution for a narrowbody aircraft operating across a wide variety of airports.

The Boeing 787 had greater design freedom, allowing Boeing to prioritize aerodynamic performance through a longer wing and swept-back raked wingtips. Its composite construction also makes it possible to develop a lightweight, flexible wing structure that works particularly well with this configuration. The absence of conventional winglets is therefore a deliberate engineering decision, not an omission.

Meanwhile, the Boeing 777X represents a different approach altogether, combining the aerodynamic advantages of an exceptionally long wing with a folding mechanism that addresses airport limitations. Its design demonstrates how manufacturers can use mechanical innovation to overcome restrictions that would otherwise prevent them from pursuing more ambitious aerodynamic improvements.

Together, these three aircraft show that there is no single ideal wingtip design for every commercial aircraft, since the most effective solution ultimately depends on the aircraft's size, intended operations, and the infrastructure it must use.

#6196. Amex Auto-Enrolling Card Members In Paperless Billing (Sorry, Dad!)

Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)…

With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:

We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

After that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

Now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it says this:

Not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary says something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress…

As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

What do you make of Amex’s switch to paperless billing?

#6195. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6193. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

Aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's new premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a new product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#6192. The Mid-Size Florida Hub Betting $1.5 Billion That Delta Air Lines Will Turn It Into An International Gateway

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Tampa International Airport (TPA) is building a $1.528 billion terminal that will add 16 gates, a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area for international arrivals, and enough capacity to handle 35 million annual passengers by 2037. Structural steel will begin going up this Summer, with completion targeted for late 2028 and a public opening in 2029. It is the airport's first new airside terminal in nearly 20 years.

Delta signed a 20-year anchor lease for at least six of those gates, including a purpose-built Delta Sky Club lounge. The commitment is the longest and most substantial terminal agreement Delta has made at any mid-size Florida airport. It positions Tampa as a potential international gateway for the airline once the new Federal Inspection Services facility gives the airport the processing capacity to support widebody international arrivals.

TPA is building its first new airside terminal in nearly 20 years. The Hillsborough County Aviation Authority Board approved the 100% final design for Airside D on February 5, clearing the project for full construction. The facility will be 600,000 square feet (55,742 sq meters) with 16 gates serving both domestic and international flights.

It includes a new Federal Inspection Services area for processing international arrivals, an 8-lane security checkpoint, and a new checked baggage inspection system in the main terminal. The total project cost is $1.528 billion, including a $902 million supplemental contract approved in late 2025.

Construction is well underway. A 300-ton crane is erecting the structural steel framework, which consists of 6,200 tons of steel comprising over 7,300 individual pieces connected by 96,000 bolts and 212,000 inches of welding. Approximately 200 workers are on site daily, with that number expected to increase significantly as the project moves from structural work into mechanical, electrical, and interior fit-out phases.

HNTB designed the project, the same firm that designed TPA's existing main terminal and automated people mover system. Completion is targeted for late 2028 with a public opening in 2029. Once operational, Airside D will increase TPA's total gate count and expand the airport's annual passenger capacity from its current 25 million to 35 million by 2037.

The airport handled approximately 24 million passengers in 2024, meaning it is approaching the capacity limits of its existing terminal complex. Airside D provides the infrastructure to accommodate the growth TPA has been experiencing without the crowding and gate constraints that would otherwise limit airline expansion at the airport.

Delta was selected as the anchor tenant for Airside D in a decision announced by the Hillsborough County Aviation Authority. The lease covers at least six of the 16 gates on a 20-year term, giving Delta a dedicated presence in the new facility through approximately 2049. The agreement includes a mezzanine-level Delta Sky Club, the carrier's first purpose-built lounge at TPA.

The remaining 10 gates will be available for other carriers, with the airport authority retaining flexibility to assign them based on demand and airline interest. A 20-year anchor lease at a mid-size airport is not a routine commitment. Delta operates from dozens of airports across the United States, but it signs long-term anchor agreements only at facilities where it intends to build or sustain a significant operation over multiple decades.

The lease term matches the terminal's useful life, meaning Delta is committing to Tampa for as long as Airside D operates. The Sky Club inclusion signals that Delta expects enough premium traffic at TPA to justify the capital investment and ongoing operating cost of a dedicated lounge, which the airline typically reserves for its largest hubs and busiest focus cities.

Delta currently operates approximately 45 daily departures from Tampa to destinations including Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis-St. Paul, Salt Lake City, New York-JFK, Boston, and Amsterdam. The Amsterdam route, operated on the A330-900, is Delta's first year-round widebody international service from TPA.

It serves as a proof of concept for the kind of European flying the airline could expand from Airside D once the facility opens. The six-gate commitment in a terminal with a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area positions Delta to add additional international routes from Tampa without competing for gate space or customs processing capacity in the airport's existing international facility.

Delta operates the largest domestic hub-and-spoke network of any US carrier. It is built around hubs at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta Airport (ATL), Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC), Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

Atlanta is the largest by a wide margin, handling over 1,000 daily Delta departures and serving as the airline's primary connecting hub for domestic and international traffic. Delta's existing Florida footprint is substantial but spread across multiple airports without a dominant hub presence at any single one.

The airline operates from Orlando International Airport (MCO), Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Miami International Airport (MIA), Jacksonville International Airport (JAX), and TPA, among others. None of those airports functions as a Delta hub in the way that Atlanta or Detroit do.

However, Orlando and Fort Lauderdale carry the highest Florida frequencies, driven by leisure demand from Delta's Northeastern and Midwestern hubs. The anchor tenant commitment does not make Tampa a hub. Delta is not building a connecting operation at TPA comparable to what it runs at Atlanta or Detroit.

The lease establishes Tampa as a long-term focus city with dedicated infrastructure, a premium lounge, and the physical capacity to grow well beyond the 45 daily departures Delta currently operates. The distinction matters because a focus city with a 20-year lease and a purpose-built Sky Club receives a different level of investment and scheduling priority than a station where the airline operates from shared gates on short-term agreements.

TPA already handles international flights. Edelweiss serves Zurich, Avianca recently launched daily service to Bogota, and Delta added year-round Amsterdam service. Caribbean and Canadian routes to destinations including San Juan, Toronto, Montreal, Cancun, and Santo Domingo operate from the existing terminal.

The airport is not starting international service from zero. What it lacks is the capacity to grow it meaningfully beyond what the current Federal Inspection Services facility can process. Airside D's dedicated FIS area changes that constraint. The new facility will have its own Customs and Border Protection processing area capable of handling widebody international arrivals simultaneously with domestic operations on the same concourse.

Delta's six gates in a terminal with FIS capability give the airline the infrastructure to operate international flights from Tampa without competing for processing capacity in the airport's existing international arrivals facility. Routes to London, Paris, or additional European destinations that require a full international arrivals hall become operationally feasible in a way they are not today from Delta's current gate positions.

The most striking figure in the airport authority's route development materials is the leakage rate. Approximately 50% of Tampa's international origin-and-destination traffic currently uses other Florida airports, primarily MIA, MCO, and FLL.

Tampa Bay area residents flying internationally drive to other airports because nonstop international options from TPA are limited. Airside D's FIS capacity, combined with Delta's anchor presence and the gate infrastructure to support widebody international service, is designed to recapture that leakage by giving Tampa the facilities to offer the international routes its local market already demands.

Everyone from first-timers to frequent flyers should be aware of these alterations.

The Tampa Bay metropolitan area is one of the fastest-growing regions in the US. The four-county metro area comprising Hillsborough, Pinellas, Pasco, and Hernando counties has added over 400,000 residents since 2010 and now exceeds 3.3 million people. The region's economy has diversified beyond its traditional tourism and military base.

Indeed, the finance, healthcare, technology, and logistics sectors are driving corporate travel demand alongside the leisure traffic that has historically defined Florida aviation. TPA handled 24.5 million passengers in fiscal year 2025, approaching the 25 million capacity ceiling the airport authority identified as the trigger point for Airside D.

The 2029 opening timing aligns with several fleet developments at Delta. Namely, Delta's Airbus A350-1000 deliveries will begin in late 2026, freeing up A330-900s and A350-900s that could be deployed on international routes from secondary hubs and focus cities, including Tampa.

Delta's year-round Amsterdam service, launched on the A330-900, is a proof of concept for European widebody service from TPA. If the route performs well through 2027 and 2028, additional European destinations from Airside D's gates become a natural extension of the strategy once the facility opens.

#6190. Hah: Emirates Puts Auditors On Flights To “Provide Support & Guidance” To Crew

Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service issues at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a new initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants…

Emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a new initiative involving this small group of employees:

On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers…

A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha)

Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

It goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

When it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”

As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”

I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”

There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

Why would an auditor on board create stress? If you are doing what you are supposed to be doing, then there would not be a problem. That auditor that write up how wonderfully well you performed your duties and are ready for promotion.

I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. On those flights I wear a uniform and am additional to the crew complement and my role is to support and to a lesser degree assess member of my flying team. I find it really beneficial as airline crew are typically remote workers and rarely have access to their ground manager. It also gives me the ability to see first hand lots of the pain points my team complain to me about - service routines, galley layouts etc. I don't think these kind of roles are that unusual in the airline world. We just aren't called 'Standard Pursers' ouch.

If they're not "working" the flight, I could perceive this not going well with customers as well in a way: if you see people constantly passing by you and never checking on you, or if you ask that person for help and they direct it to another person, then it could come across the wrong way. Imagine you press the call attendant button and the Standard Purser just walks right by you. You'd probably think that you're being ignored by staff / they're slacking off.

If only all airlines had in-flight service auditors, the skies would be a better place.

#6188. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

#6187. Lockheed’s CL-1201 Was A Nuclear-Powered Flying Aircraft Carrier That Never Left The Drawing Board

In the early jet era, Lockheed had a full docket of pioneering aerospace programs, but even among the iconic airplanes in the Skunk Works portfolio, the CL-1201 stands out for its scale and ambition. Locked in the endlessly escalating arms race with the Soviet Union, the US Air Force has commissioned an engineering study into a flying, nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. On September 12, 1969, Lockheed engineers G. Daniel Brewer, S. Dalton, and P. J. Sibley filed a company report LR-22802, outlining a machine that seemed to defy physics.

It was a nearly 6,000-ton (5,375 metric tons) flying wing that spanned 1,120 feet (341 meters) in an audacious technical leap to rewrite strategic air mobility and power projection over foreign soil. The mothership was expected to haul at least 22 McDonnell Douglas fighter jets on massive underwing pylons in the same way that the smaller planes carried missiles. Designated the CL-1201, the behemoth 'lightning' carrier would be capable of reaching any conflict zone in hours and promised to cruise for 41 straight days without resupply.

Although the aerodynamics and physics of constructing such a flying colossus sound like the greatest technical hurdle to its success, the failure of its nuclear power source stopped any progress. Popular accounts of the program claim that the USAF did in fact commission an active service example. However, no records to date, including the most detailed public file NASA, recorded as Memorandum X-2386, show that any order was officially lodged.

The CL-1201's propulsion abandoned standard jet fuel logistics in favor of an unproven liquid-metal-cooled reactor delivering 1,830 megawatts of thermal energy. That staggering heat drove four mammoth aft turbofans at Mach 0.8 at 30,000 feet (9,144 meters), offering effectively unlimited global range. The design aimed to bypass the need for any overseas airfields and reliance on allied partners entirely by maintaining an airborne presence for over a month, limited only by crew endurance and engine oil.

The primary CL-1201-1-1 Attack Aircraft Carrier variant would house a crew of 845 to operate 22 fighters beneath its wings. Meanwhile, the alternative CL-1201-1-3 Logistics Support Aircraft traded strike fighters for a cavernous cargo bay. It was proposed with the capacity to deploy an entire combat brigade of 3,896 soldiers with 6,207 tons (5,631 metric tons) of equipment to any hot spot on the globe.

Eight years before Lockheed's engineers filed their report, US President John F. Kennedy had already canceled the US aircraft nuclear propulsion program. After 15 years of research, it was finally called off in 1961. The numbers had never successfully solved all the safety issues with installing an active nuclear reactor in an airplane. Two airships, the USS Akron and Macon, preceded the C-1201 as early motherships, and one Convair NB-36H had been equipped with nuclear power plants for test flights.

Yet, scientists were unable to ever create an atomic engine considered safe enough to not have a devastating environmental impact in the event of a mishap. Furthermore, turning the CL-1201 concept into an airworthy airframe demanded solving the immediate physics problem of how to lift nearly 12 million lb (5.4 million kg) into the sky. No airport on Earth could handle the landing gear footprint, forcing the design team to adopt a complex propulsion compromise.

The retrieval system of the CL-1201 lowered a hydraulically stabilized pantograph hook 35 feet (10.7 meters) beneath the airframe into clean, undisturbed air. A docking fighter pilot engaged the hook with a dorsal latch, allowing heavy winches to haul the aircraft up against cradle stops before swinging it into internal maintenance bays. This acrobatic aerial recovery demanded precision flying in high-altitude crosswinds, turning routine combat patrols into dangerous flight-test maneuvers that risked pilot lives.

Docking a 40,000-lb (18,140 kg) fighter beneath a 125,000-square-foot (11,613 sq m) wing generated lethal aerodynamic turbulence that tested the limits of human piloting. Incoming flight crews had to fly through a violent boundary layer wake and wingtip vortex wash, with velocity spikes exceeding 120 feet (37 meters) per second. The chaotic upwash threatened to smash approaching jets against the lower wing skin, prompting designers to engineer an articulated trapeze boom.

Beyond the docking challenges, Cold War missile advances made the carrier extraordinarily vulnerable to long-range Soviet surface-to-air missile networks. The tailless 560-foot (171-meter) airframe would look like staring into the sun on an enemy's radar scope. Its gigantic profile would create an immense radar target that air defense systems like the Soviet S-200 Angara could spot hundreds of miles away. A single missile strike could instantly wipe out an entire combat wing and crack open the central atomic reactor.

A look at the number of people that power the mission of the USAF's E-4B Nightwatch.

At a gross weight of 11.85 million lb (5.4 million kg), roughly fifteen times the mass of a Boeing 747 or Lockheed C-5 Galaxy, the CL-1201 exceeded the limits of every runway in the world. Standard concrete aprons would be crushed under its landing gear, while constructing dedicated five-mile runways around the world negated the strategic autonomy that justified it. To eliminate runway dependence, engineering lead Brewer and his team adopted an extreme vertical takeoff and landing design.

Rather than routing reactor thermal energy to lift fans, the configuration housed 182 dedicated jet-fuel-powered turbojets in retractable forward fuselage bays and inner wing banks. It would dramatically scale up the multi-engine vertical lift concept of experimental aircraft at the time, like the Dornier Do 31 and Yakovlev Yak 38. Each turbine was rated for 90,000 pounds of thrust for a combined vertical output of 16.38 million pounds.

In operational practice, this propulsion created severe liabilities at every launch site. Simultaneous ignition of 182 lift jets projected a 1,400°F downward exhaust plume capable of spalling reinforced concrete, liquefying asphalt, and generating severe foreign object damage hazards across massive areas. Furthermore, the lift engines would consume nearly 1.9 million lb (0.8 million kg) of JP-5 fuel during a single five-minute departure sequence, burning the equivalent fuel capacity of six fully loaded C-5 Galaxies before the nuclear engines engaged.

Additionally, synchronizing 182 independent turbines during the low-speed transition from jet-borne hover to wing-borne aerodynamic flight introduced an alarmingly long list of potential failure points. A compressor stall or flameout within an outboard wing bank would generate violent asymmetric roll moments far exceeding the control authority of aerodynamic flight surfaces at near-zero airspeed. Ultimately, the CL 1201 was simply unviable due to its inability to break away from conventional infrastructure and limitations because of its size and not its power source, relegating the concept to a Cold War 'flight of fancy.'

The flying gas stations that kept the fastest crewed jet in history airborne and on mission.

In the 1940s and 1950s, the USAF and Atomic Energy Commission spent roughly $1 billion over 15 years on the Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion (ANP) program, hoping to build bombers that could stay airborne for weeks. The Convair NB-36H Crusader flew 47 test missions over Texas and New Mexico carrying an operational, air-cooled 1-to-3 megawatt reactor in its aft bomb bay. The bomber's entire nose had a 12-ton lead and rubber shield, complete with 12-inch-thick lead-glass windows.

Adding the 17.5-ton reactor meant the aircraft had to haul nearly 30 tons of nuclear hardware and shielding before carrying any weapons. Every test flight was shadowed by a C-97 transport plane carrying a platoon of US Marines trained to parachute into the crash site and cordon off radioactive debris. Engineers could not solve the dilemma of making a reactor light enough without sacrificing containment. Furthermore, advances in intercontinental ballistic missiles and aerial refueling made nuclear bombers strategically obsolete.

Lockheed aimed to overcome those limitations with an atomic propulsion plant rated at an astonishing 5,470 megawatts in a dual-circuit closed loop. Liquid lithium circulated through the primary reactor core at temperatures reaching 2,000°F (1,093°C), carrying thermal energy into an intermediate heat exchanger mounted inside a central structural containment cell. The secondary circuit circulated non-radioactive liquid alloy through pipes to four massive trailing-edge turbofans.

The engines used single-stage titanium fan disks spanning an unprecedented 28 feet (8.5 meters) across. The liquid metal radiators sat directly behind the 14-stage axial compressors, transferring heat into the compressed air stream to produce 300,000 pounds of thrust (1,334 kN) per engine. Containing the energy required a titanium keel and trusses that were eight inches (20 cm) thick, as well as a shield of lead, tungsten, and borated water weighing 1.2 million lb (544,300 kg).

How the Raider fixed the same R&D model of the priciest USAF plane ever made.

Commissioned in the early 1930s, the USS Akron (ZRS-4) and her sister ship USS Macon (ZRS-5) were 785-foot-long rigid helium airships. Each airship housed an internal hangar bay holding up to five Curtiss F9C-2 Sparrowhawk biplanes. To launch, a mechanical 'trapeze' lowered a fighter beneath the airship's hull into the slipstream, where the pilot released a skyhook and flew away. To recover, the pilot matched the airship's 70-knot speed and snagged the trapeze bar with a hook mounted above the upper wing.

On April 4, 1933, the Akron was caught in a violent thunderstorm off the coast of New Jersey. Downdrafts forced the tail into the Atlantic Ocean, breaking the airship apart. Less than two years later, on February 12, 1935, the Macon encountered a storm off Point Sur, California. Wind shear tore away her upper tail fin, puncturing rear gas cells and causing her to lose buoyancy and settle into the Pacific.

Before the tragic and catastrophic demise of each airship, the trapeze system actually worked well, and the Navy never lost a plane during an in-flight catch. Despite successful fighter operations, the loss of the Macon ended the US Navy's permanent pursuit of flying aircraft carriers, and there's no indication that they ever showed interest in the massive Lockheed concept. Meanwhile, the CL-1201 aimed to take this ill-fated earlier attempt and supersize it.

#6186. Bilt Rent Day Promotion December 2026: JetBlue Mosaic Status Challenge

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a new month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal). It’s interesting to see a second month in a row with no transfer bonus…

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:

Let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

The status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:

Regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

#6184. Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:

After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”

So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day…

Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

That feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that…

Best thing about them: Their livery. Stunning!. In person even better.

I flew from GRU to LHR on BA in about 2018, first class redemption. I don't remember a long passport queue, but I do remember that I was escorted by the check-in agent from the desk to the lounge which I found surprising, but could explain the lack of issues. Have the rules changed, or have air France not worked out how to bypass the queue?

LATAM is no better. I had to fight tooth and nail with them at AEP over baggage allowances. I finally got a stupervisor and quoted actual tariff rules. She was a bit shocked and quickly backed off. Average Joe would not have not known what they were trying to pull. LATAM is just another ULCC that happens to fly international.

#6183. Why United Airlines Is The Only US Carrier Left With An Overseas Hub

In general, the US legacy carriers primarily operate their networks within the continental US. All of American Airlines' ten hub airports are located within the continental US, as are all of Delta's nine hub airports. United Airlines, however, has seven hub airports in the continental US, as well as a hub in Guam, an overseas territory of the US located thousands of miles away from Washington. It's the only such operation by any US airline, and it carries on the legacy of an operation that goes back nearly 60 years.

United currently operates up to 12 daily flights to 15 different destinations in five countries out of Guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM). It is the start/end for the carrier's famous 'Island Hopper' service, and the airline also runs direct services from GUM to San Francisco with a stopover in Honolulu. This route uses a Boeing 777-300ER, while the rest of the GUM routes use the Boeing 737. United is by far the largest airline serving Guam, and it also serves as a vital link connecting Guam to the outside world.

In 1968, Continental Airlines and regional shareholders established Air Micronesia, initially headquartered in the Northern Mariana Islands. Operating under the callsign 'Air Mike', the airline initially operated Boeing 727s and became a crucial component in the region's economic development during the late 20th century. Air Micronesia held a near monopoly in the market, and its 727s were crucial in connecting what were previously remote islands to the outside world.

Continental would eventually own 100% of Air Micronesia, rebranding the airline to 'Continental Micronesia' while the headquarters eventually shifted to Guam. While other airlines attempted to connect Guam to the US at certain points and others served Micronesia from foreign countries, Continental Micronesia was by far the largest airline in this market. Among its most famous routes was the 'Island Hopper', connecting Guam to Honolulu with five stopovers, and the airline also had a substantial international network.

In 1999, Continental Micronesia began transitioning from using the 727 to the 737NG for most operations, and in 2003, the Guam International Airport Facility pushed commuter airlines out of GUM's Commuter Terminal and leased the facility to Continental. The airline would become Guam's largest private-sector employer, while connecting GUM to over 20 destinations.

In 2010, Continental Airlines announced that it would merge with United Airlines, keeping the United name. In 2017, Continental Micronesia was formally merged into United Airlines (it had previously operated as a subsidiary of United Continental Holdings), and today, all Guam flights are directly operated by United.

Airlines are hardly afraid of shutting down unprofitable hubs, and United itself dehubbed the Cleveland hub that it also inherited from Continental during the merger in 2014. However, the Guam operations were making money for the airline, and they're a vital link to the communities served. In addition, United absolutely dominates Guam, and the hub offers a unique strategic position within the carrier's network that couldn't otherwise be replicated by another hub.

Guam itself is a hub for lucrative military and government activity, and United's position in Guam means that it essentially receives all government travel contracts. Because of the airline's dominance in GUM, it can also charge high fares due to the lack of competition. Altogether, Guam is actually one of United's most lucrative hubs, even if it is also one of its smallest. The operation makes the airline money, and so it will remain a United hub, even as other US legacy carriers have dehubbed their hubs outside of the US mainland.

Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD)

Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR)

Guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM)

San Francisco International Airport (SFO)

Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH)

Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD)

In March 2026, the carrier began transitioning from using the 737-800 to the 737 MAX 8 for its Guam operations, with the switch having been completed in October. These ten aircraft feature a significantly upgraded interior compared to the old 737-800s, and they feature signs in English and Japanese rather than English and Spanish, while the front row of economy can be collapsed to accommodate a stretcher for medevac flights. In addition, two United First seats are blocked on the Island Hopper to be used as a pilot crew rest facility.

United uniquely operates routes within Asia. Here's why it does this.

Going into the 2010s, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines both operated hubs at Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT). These hubs had operated for decades (Delta inherited NRT operations from Northwest Airlines, while United acquired the NRT routes from Pan Am) and essentially connected US passengers to Asia, serving as a central hub. But in the mid-2010s, United gradually discontinued intra-Asia routes out of NRT, and Delta exited NRT entirely in 2020 (it will return in 2027 with a single route from Seattle).

Whereas United's Guam hub primarily serves the local market, the NRT hubs operated by United and Delta mainly existed for connections. However, the arrival of the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 allowed these airlines to serve more destinations in Asia nonstop from the US, and nonstop flights typically earn a fare premium over one-stop options. As such, the NRT hubs weren't necessary anymore, since they were essentially set up due to range limitations of older widebodies like the Boeing 747-200.

In addition to the improved economics of new widebody aircraft, United announced a joint venture with All Nippon Airways in 2011, while Delta announced a joint venture with Korean Air in 2017. With these, the intra-Asia routes are covered by their joint venture partners, eliminating the need to operate these flights with their own metal. In other words, United's NRT hub has been replaced by nonstop flights to Asia and ANA's operations out of Tokyo, while Delta's NRT hub has been replaced by Korean Air's hub in Seoul.

Apart from the carrier's one-stop flight from GUM to San Francisco via Honolulu with the 777-300ER, all of United's Guam routes now use the 737 MAX 8. There are currently ten of them stationed in GUM, and they operate to Taipei, Manila, Airai, Saipan, Yap, Pohnpei, Chuuk, Tokyo Narita, Tokyo Haneda, Osaka, and Nagoya. In addition, the airline's flight to Airai continues to Manila on some days of the week, while the flight to Chuuk is part of the Island Hopper, flying from Guam to Honolulu via Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, Kwajalein, and Majuro.

Several of these routes do not operate daily, as local demand is ultimately limited and the 737 MAX 8 is a relatively large aircraft, able to carry up to 166 passengers in United's configuration. Japan is United's largest market out of GUM, as it connects the airport to four airports in Japan while operating up to five daily flights between GUM and Japan. Notably, United does not serve Nagoya from the mainland US nonstop.

Some of these routes can be extremely long, which makes the fuel savings of the 737 MAX 8 over the 737-800 highly impactful. Meanwhile, the 777-300ER is flown to Guam almost entirely due to strong demand for cargo, as this is the aircraft in United's fleet with the highest cargo capacity. The airline only has 22 of these planes, which make up less than 10% of its overall widebody fleet, and yet the cargo revenue is strong enough to justify its use on the San Francisco-Honolulu-Guam route.

United Airlines invests in cutting-edge technology and sleek design for its Guam hub, but what surprises await travelers?

While United's Guam operations have generally been successful, the hub has been facing difficulties in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as a decline in demand from Japan, the largest market for the hub. Ordinarily, United may simply shift capacity to another hub, but that isn't easy to do with Guam. The airport is thousands of miles away from any of United's other hubs, the carrier has a pilot and flight attendant base in Guam, and the ten 737s are specially configured for these services.

What United has done with these assets is move them back to NRT. In recent years, the carrier has launched new fifth freedom routes from NRT to Cebu, Kaohsiung, and Ulaanbaatar, using the flight numbers of the carrier's nonstop flights to NRT from the mainland US and operating the flights with Guam-based 737s. Crucially, these destinations are not served by ANA, which means that United is expanding the joint venture's Asia coverage while deploying assets that would have otherwise been underutilized.

It's one of the most creative ways to utilize assets when the standard operation is no longer producing the returns that it once did. Not only that, but the airline has generated tremendous excitement and publicity over these routes, with the Ulaanbaatar route standing out in particular, and this is beneficial for loyalty program and credit card sign-ups, which is where the carrier makes its real money.
