The may be the entry-level card option for Atmos Rewards, but it's anything but basic. This card packs a punch with a free checked bag and preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flights, with a fan-favorite $99 Companion Fare for cardholders who meet the spending requirements.

Even if you don't fly Alaska or Hawaiian often, the points you earn on the card can help you get outsized value. With a robust network of Oneworld and nonalliance partners, Atmos Rewards can take you just about anywhere in the world. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The is a cobranded airline card within Atmos Rewards, the joint loyalty program between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

For a $95 annual fee, the card earns valuable Atmos Rewards points and provides a few added benefits.

Some of the best ways to maximize these points include redeeming for premium cabins with Oneworld partners, such as Cathay Pacific and Fiji Airways. However, Atmos Rewards points are also solid for short-haul domestic routes on Alaska Airlines and American Airlines.

One of the card's standout perks is its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) that is earned each account anniversary as long as you've spent $6,000 or more in the prior anniversary year.

Generally, it's a solid option for Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines frequent flyers, thanks to the perks provided when flying with either airline, such as free checked bags and preferred boarding.

However, if you're looking for more premium perks like lounge access, this card won't meet your needs.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Alaska Airlines flights?

The offers fewer benefits than other cobranded airline cards. However, you can still expect some perks.

Cardholders receive one piece of free checked luggage for themselves and up to six other passengers on the same reservation when flying Alaska or Hawaiian and paying with the Atmos Rewards Ascent. That can save $45 per person each way on most itineraries, though the first checked bag still costs $30 on intra-Hawaii flights.

Cardholders also get preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian, and they'll receive 20% back on inflight purchases with both airlines when they use the card.

If you're working toward Atmos Rewards status, you can earn 1 status point for every $3 spent on the card, with no cap on the number of status points you can earn through spending.

As mentioned above, one of the best benefits of the Atmos Rewards Ascent is the $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23). This can be unlocked after spending $6,000 or more on the card within the prior anniversary year.

You'll get value from this perk as long as you fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines with a friend or family member on paid fares at least once a year.

Carly Helfand, TPG's director of content strategy, previously used the Ascent's Companion Fare to take a last-minute trip to Chicago with her husband. The round-trip flights from Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) cost $542.60 per person, but she paid $679.63 for both tickets thanks to the Companion Fare.

While the Atmos Rewards Ascent doesn't provide outright lounge access, you can get $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership when you pay with this card. A membership costs $795 per year.

This benefit alone offsets the card's $95 annual fee. However, given how expensive membership is, this perk isn't too useful unless you were already going to pay for an Alaska Lounge+ membership.

It's worth noting that this card doesn't provide basic travel protections like baggage delay insurance, lost luggage insurance, purchase protection and trip cancellation/interruption coverage. If these perks are important to you, you may want to consider an alternative option.

On a more positive note, this is a good card to take abroad since it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees.

Related: The 5 best airline credit cards with annual fees of $150 or less

The earns Atmos Rewards points on purchases. These points are often best redeemed toward air travel. Let's dive into what to know.

Plus, cardholders with an eligible Bank of America account will also receive a 10% bonus on all points earned from purchases.

TPG's November 2026 valuations estimate Atmos Rewards points are worth 1.6 cents apiece.

This card may not be the best option for spending categories outside of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. However, if you're all in on earning Atmos Rewards points, swiping this card becomes more attractive.

Atmos Rewards provides stellar redemption rates on domestic travel. Short-haul economy tickets start at just 4,500 points one-way.

One of my favorite ways to redeem Atmos Rewards points is to book short-haul American Airlines flights, such as Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) to Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (SDF) in Kentucky, at this 4,500-point rate.

It can also be a good deal to redeem for longer domestic flights. For example, a one-way flight from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) starts at 12,500 points in economy.

Premium cabins can start as low as 15,000 points one-way on shorter flights and 30,000 points one-way on longer U.S. routes. For trips to Hawaii, awards from the West Coast typically start at 12,500 points each way in economy and 30,000 points each way in first class.

Atmos Rewards is part of the Oneworld alliance, which means you can book partner flights with airlines such as British Airways, Cathay Pacific and Qantas. Keep in mind that partner awards include a $20 nonrefundable booking fee.

TPG director of travel content Eric Rosen's favorite ways to maximize Atmos Rewards redemptions include booking Cathay Pacific or Japan Airlines business class from the U.S. to Asia for 75,000 points one-way and Fiji Airways business class from the U.S. to Fiji for 75,000 points one-way.

Related: 10 best ways to redeem 100,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points

Despite its benefits, there are a few reasons why you may not want to apply to the $95-annual-fee :

If you are ready to go all in on Atmos Rewards, consider its premium sibling: the .

For a higher $395 annual fee, the card provides eight Alaska Lounge passes each calendar year, a 25,000-point Global Companion Award each account anniversary and a high earning rate on foreign purchases.

Learn more in our full review of the Atmos Rewards Summit Visa.

Related: How to reach Alaska Airlines elite status with the Atmos Summit Visa

The is a great way to collect valuable Atmos Rewards points. If you value that currency highly, this card is a fantastic starting point.

However, if you find the earning rates restrictive and the benefits underwhelming, another option may be the best choice.

Related: Atmos Rewards Ascent vs. Business: Which $95 Alaska-Hawaiian card should you get?

New cardholders can earn 70,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $2,500 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. TPG values this bonus at $1,120, not including the value of the Companion Fare.

This is a really strong offer, but not the absolute highest we've seen in the card's offer history. Still, it's high enough that I wouldn't hesitate to apply if the timing otherwise makes sense for your personal finances.

Award-savvy travelers know you don't have to be an Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines loyalist to enjoy the rewards you earn with this card. However, some of the card's perks may go unused if you don't at least occasionally fly with one of its primary airlines.

Consider what matters most to you in exchange for a $95 annual fee, and you'll be on your way to hitting the skies.

#6137. United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

United Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather. Three years later, they’re admitting it was all a lie. I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight plan and the airline insisting on a weather diversion. Now, Live and Let’s Fly flags the airline chairman’s admission that the passengers’ explanation was right. Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17. A dispatcher had entered the wrong destination in the paperwork. The pilots flew there. The flight attendants apparently believed they’d reached the city everyone bought tickets to. He described the weather explanation as “just a lie” and offered this advice: “The best way of public relations is to tell the truth, but tell it responsibly.” Passengers Were Welcomed To Abuja While Sitting In Asaba On November 26, 2023, flight 0504 left Lagos with passengers booked to Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. It landed in Asaba instead, about 200 miles away. This was United Nigeria Airlines, not United Airlines. Passengers reported that the flight attendants welcomed everyone to Abuja but then everyone discovered where they actually were. November 26, 2023 — Peacock (@dawisu) Another passenger shared video: We legit got scared sha. Laff wan kee me 😅 pic.twitter.com/sWxbnJeDna— Lord Macky (@AugustineMacky) November 26, 2023 The airline’s original statement blamed “poor destination weather”, said the pilot knew about the diversion, and attributed the confusion to an incorrect cabin announcement. The plane eventually continued to Abuja. The Investigation Uncovered The Truth The flight used an Airbus A320 operated by Bulgaria’s Fly2Sky for United Nigeria Airlines. Fly2Sky said at the time that United Nigeria had assigned it a Lagos–Asaba flight the previous day and hadn’t requested a change during the pilots’ preflight briefing. The Nigerian regulator identified failures well beyond one person entering a destination incorrectly. In its findings there was: Poor coordination between United Nigeria’s operations center and the company supplying the aircraft. No joint preflight briefing between the pilots and flight attendants. United Nigeria’s failure to monitor the leased aircraft through its operations center. Failure to follow the approved flight plan filed with air traffic control. The chairman story is about a dispatch error. The regulator, though, laid out several opportunities to prevent it. British Airways Has Done It, Too In March 2019, a British Airways flight scheduled from London City to Düsseldorf went to Edinburgh after the pilots received paperwork for the wrong destination. The passengers had bought a flight to Germany but the flight took them to Scotland. A few weeks later, Scandinavian Airlines sent a Copenhagen–Florence flight to Bologna. That was a deliberate decision made before departure because the pilots lacked the correct routing information for Florence. They flew to Bologna with plans to bus passengers onward. It’s just that they kept this information to themselves. And in August 2025, I covered AirAsia X passengers being welcomed to Incheon after their Kuala Lumpur flight landed at Seoul’s Gimpo airport, about 20 miles away. Here’s the Instagram video from that coverage: View the video shared by @rizalhakimm_punyer on Instagram AirAsia X said it had intentionally diverted for fuel because bad weather had caused congestion at Incheon. It acknowledged an incorrect cabin announcement, said the captain corrected it, and offered travel vouchers. Okonkwo also used his conference appearance to discuss a passenger upset that an advertised 11:30 a.m. flight had left at 11:20. He said he’d initially wanted to shout back, but instead responded, “I apologise for United Nigeria Airline leaving on time.” An airline chairman giving a speech about accurately convey what on-time means. The chairman story is about a dispatch error. The regulator, though, laid out several opportunities to prevent it.

In March 2019, a British Airways flight scheduled from London City to Düsseldorf went to Edinburgh after the pilots received paperwork for the wrong destination. The passengers had bought a flight to Germany but the flight took them to Scotland. A few weeks later, Scandinavian Airlines sent a Copenhagen–Florence flight to Bologna. That was a deliberate decision made before departure because the pilots lacked the correct routing information for Florence. They flew to Bologna with plans to bus passengers onward. It’s just that they kept this information to themselves. And in August 2025, I covered AirAsia X passengers being welcomed to Incheon after their Kuala Lumpur flight landed at Seoul’s Gimpo airport, about 20 miles away. It acknowledged an incorrect cabin announcement, said the captain corrected it, and offered travel vouchers. #6136. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6135. Florida Passenger Barred By American Airlines—She Kicks Police, Spits In An Officer’s Face

An American Airlines passenger was arrested in Florida on nine charges after being denied boarding. Police say she refused to leave the Tampa airport terminal, chest bumped one officer, kicked another in the chest, and spat in a third officer’s face. Ana L. Gianaras, 34, of Grayslake, Illinois, was arrested around 3 p.m. November 8 in Airside F according to the affidavit. Guessing Headlights reported the arrest and obtained the police and court records. The booking photo comes from the Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office: Police say Gianaras yelled, cursing and screaming and that her speech was slurred and her breath smelled of alcohol. She was sitting at a bar when, according to the affidavit, she got off her barstool and struck one of the officer’s chest with her own. That’s when officers say they tried to arrest her. She tensed up and tried to pull away as they struggled to handcuff her. During a search, she allegedly kicked another officer in the chest with a “reverse single leg kick.” Then, as another officer attempted to place her in the rear seat of a patrol car, police say she turned and spat in his face. Police say they found: Five cannabis cigarettes. Two plastic tubes containing suspected THC oil. 6.9 grams of orange pills identified as 30 milligram Adderall tablets. The affidavit reports preliminary positive field tests for the cannabis and oil and that she couldn’t produce a prescription for the Adderall. And once she made it to jail, sheriff’s deputies used a Taser but it’s not clear why. Her charges break down as: Six felonies: three counts of battery on a law enforcement officer, one count of resisting an officer with violence, and two counts of controlled substance possession involving the Adderall and THC oil. Three misdemeanors: disorderly intoxication, resisting an officer without violence, and possession of less than 20 grams of cannabis. She was booked at 5:21 p.m. on November 8. At her first appearance the next day, the court set bonds totaling $26,150. After two nights in jail, she was released November 10 on bond. I’ve covered an American Airlines passenger at Dallas-Fort Worth who was denied boarding for apparent intoxication and then attacked three gate agents with her phone. And there was the Orlando passenger who fled on a motorized suitcase after being refused boarding and allegedly spat at an officer. If American’s employees saw the same signs of intoxication described by police, keeping Gianaras off the plane was the right call. Their side of the story though isn’t clear. I reached out to American Airlines, and they did not respond. In recent years, first-class, business-class and premium economy have stolen many of the headlines when it comes to air travel — and there’s a big reason for that.

Airlines have leaned heavily into premium seating, with the fancy suites and recliners serving as the biggest money-makers on the plane.

That has led to a ton of luxe new suites and features, like United's Polaris Studios which debuted earlier this year with 27-inch screens.

At the same time, we’re also seeing some intriguing new innovations in economy, too.

To be clear, the seats aren’t suddenly getting wider, and the legroom isn’t magically improving.

But a growing number of airlines are rolling out some new options and upgrades that should ultimately lead to more enjoyable flights, without the need to pay thousands of dollars (or hundreds of thousands of points).

For starters, there’s the Wi-Fi. It has long been a pain point for travelers, as they'd be stuck paying a fee for an often-spotty service.

Nearly all of the large U.S. carriers now offer — or have plans to offer — on-board internet free to members of their loyalty programs.

Most U.S. airlines are installing or preparing to install ultrafast service from Starlink, which is widely regarded as the fastest Wi-Fi in the sky today.

The days of being disconnected when you fly are fast disappearing.

Whenever I sleep on a red-eye flight in coach, I tend to wake up with a sore neck.

This year, Emirates debuted a new feature that should help.

Its "U-Dream" setup has side wings that cradle your neck as you sleep. You can see what it looks like below.

Swipe to see me trying out a "generic" version of the concept at an aviation conference last year.

If you're going to be in economy, that headrest looks like it would definitely make the experience more comfortable — especially on a long flight from the U.S. to Dubai.

Walk-up snack bars are popping up on some commercial planes, which double as a way to stretch your legs during a long flight — and get some sustenance at 35,000 feet.

United used the last row of its new Airbus A321XLR for a snack bar, which will be a nice option for passengers flying that single-aisle plane on long-haul routes.

A handful of additional U.S. carriers have announced plans to offer their snack bars in the sky in the near future. JetBlue has offered a snack "pantry" for years on its long-range planes.

Don’t want to splurge on a pricey business-class or premium economy seat?

United recently announced it would join Air New Zealand in offering a couch, of sorts, in economy.

Next year, the carrier plans to debut a product it’s calling its “Relax Row” on some long-haul flights.

Available as a paid add-on, the concept allows you to turn three economy seats into one "bed." The airline has framed this as a strong option for families traveling together.

The setup is similar to the “Skycouch" Air New Zealand has offered on its long transpacific flights for years.

United plans to outfit some of its largest twin-aisle jets with the “Relax Row,” including some Boeing 777 and 787 aircraft.

How much would you pay for a few hours of shut-eye?

Air New Zealand plans to one-up itself soon with a new bunk-bed in coach.

The new “Skynest” concept will feature two sets of bunk beds stacked three high, with a ladder to reach the upper bunks.

Passengers will be able to book a four-hour nap for an additional fee of $495.

It’s not business-class, but if your only goal is to get some sleep on a long flight from the U.S. to New Zealand, it could be well worth it.

Speaking of ultra-long journeys, Qantas is preparing to launch the world’s longest flights.

Its “Project Sunrise” service from Sydney to London is scheduled to start in October 2027. The service will be followed by flights from Sydney to New York City.

On board the ultra-long-range Airbus A350-1000, passengers won’t just find new premium seating options.

There will also be a “well-being zone,” where passengers can walk around, stretch — and maybe even do a few exercises.

That movement is crucial on flights that will span nearly a full day in the air.

Meanwhile, even as passengers board with multiple screens and devices in their bags, airlines are doubling down on seatback screens.

In the U.S., they’re already a staple on United, Delta Air Lines and JetBlue.

But carriers are also upgrading their seatback entertainment with better headphone technology, streaming services and entertainment options.

United has been working to equip all of its seatback devices with Bluetooth pairing technology, which allows passengers to connect their Apple AirPods and similar devices to the screens.

The carrier also recently rolled out a new partnership with Spotify, which lets flyers stream from their accounts on the seatback screen.

Delta, meanwhile, has launched a seatback partnership with YouTube — and is preparing to deploy new, next-generation screens with a host of new inflight features.

As all of that unfolds, American is pivoting back to screens after removing them from its planes years ago. It will be some time before they are widely available, though.

Airlines have also struck up content partnerships with major newspapers (like the Delta-Wall Street Journal tie-up) and streaming platforms (like United’s with Apple TV+).

We’ve come a long way from the days when the whole plane would watch the same movie on communal screens.

#6132. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

#6131. Rakuten’s 100% Rebates Let You Buy Amex Points For 1 Cent Each—Bilt Members With Status Get Even More

Rakuten is offering 100% back on several subscriptions, which means you can effectively buy American Express Membership Rewards points for 1 cent apiece. And if you have Bilt Silver status or higher, you can receive Bilt points at the same price. That’s the option I’d choose, because Bilt points are far more valuable. These deals can make sense even if you assign no value at all to the subscription. Spend $100 on an eligible purchase and choose 10,000 points instead of the $100 rebate. You keep the service, too. And there’s a best-ever Rakuten referral offer – Rakuten is an online shopping portal that earns points or cash back for the purchases you make anywhere, akin to the mileage malls that work with airlines like American, United, Alaska, et al. You can choose between cash back, Amex points or Bilt points. The easy, quick win before this offer is just to go to GiftCards.com through the portal and buy a $50 gift card for Uber, DoorDash, Southwest Airlines or Delta. You get $50 or equivalent points back, making this a free $50 (or better, since the points can be worth more than $50). I’ve covered using Rakuten offers to acquire inexpensive Amex points for years, and this summer’s Surfshark offer worked the same way. There are several opportunities available together now. The Current Offers Doctor of Credit flags this batch of offers. Each subscription offer is limited to a new customer or first subscription purchase, with a limit of one per Rakuten member. Merchant   Rebate   Terms That Affect The Deal Coveron, formerly NordProtect   100%   All listed individual and family subscription plans qualify. If you already earned a NordProtect rebate, the name change doesn’t make you eligible again. NordVPN   100%   Only the Basic plan portion of Plus, Complete or Prime bundles earns rewards. Orders must go through the U.S. site. NordPass   100%   First subscription signup only. Other Nord products purchased through this offer don’t qualify. Incogni   95%   First subscription payment only, with a 40 day verification period. Surfshark   95%   First purchase only. Subscription extensions and free trial promotions don’t qualify. The 95% offers work out to 95 Amex points, or 95 Bilt points with status, per eligible dollar. That’s about 1.05 cents per point before tax. Coveron is especially interesting because Rakuten explicitly includes its full individual and family plans. At the prices Coveron advertises: Two years of individual Full Protection costs $239.76, which would generate 23,976 points at 100 points per dollar. Two years of Full Family Protection costs $647.76, which would generate 64,776 points. Those calculations assume the advertised price and 100% rate are what you see when you click through Rakuten. The family plan lets you acquire a larger block of points at the same price per point. Rakuten also says Coveron, NordVPN and NordPass are separate products, so you can qualify for each. That doesn’t override the requirement to be a new customer for the particular offer. Sales tax doesn’t earn the portal rebate. If your purchase attracts 8.25% tax, a 100 points per dollar offer costs about 1.08 cents per point. The rewards from the credit card you use to pay are on top of this though. Why I’d Take Bilt Points Over Amex Points When Rakuten added Bilt as a payout option, I preferred it to Membership Rewards. I still do, provided I’m getting the full conversion rate. #6129. Can Trump’s Agenda Survive the Blue Tsunami?

The core question is whether Republicans can preserve institutional gains long enough for them to become permanent.

President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., November 9, 2026.

The catastrophic midterm results dealt to Republicans two weeks ago threaten but do not ultimately negate the conservative policy landscape as it stands two years into President Trump’s second term. As I wrote before the election, many aspects of this administration are clearly good from the conservative perspective, not just by comparison to the Biden administration, but to Trump’s own first term and previous Republican administrations since the days of Ronald Reagan.

The border has been secured, deportations have been carried out at a high rate, federal agencies have been forced to abandon much of their institutional commitment to DEI and financial support of the left-wing NGO complex, universities have been put on notice that federal funding is not unconditional, and the administrative state has undergone its most serious shake-up in generations.

President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., November 9, 2026.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

On “Can Trump’s Agenda Survive the Blue Tsunami?”

#6128. United Airlines Is Now Worst For Checked Bags, Delta’s Cancellations Nearly Doubled—What The Latest Federal Data Shows

United Airlines is now worse than American at handling checked bags. Delta’s cancellation rate has nearly doubled. And American, which has spent years bumping more passengers than any other airline, cut involuntary denied boardings 84% in the third quarter. The latest federal airline statistics show some results that don’t fit the usual reputations. It also shows why calling an airline “premium” requires more than nicer seats and better wifi. Strong operational performance isn’t enough but it’s the table stakes. An airline needs to get the basics right first, including delivering bags alongside their owners, as close to on-time as possible. The Department of Transportation’s November Air Travel Consumer Report covers September and the first nine months of 2026. Here’s the domestic flight performance through September, and I take a look at how this performance compares to earlier trends. Airline   On time2025   On time2026   Canceled2025   Canceled2026 Alaska Airlines*   77.44%   78.64%   1.01%   1.30% Delta Air Lines   79.57%   78.31%   1.19%   2.25% United Airlines   76.77%   76.20%   1.34%   1.75% American Airlines   73.09%   73.30%   2.57%   2.99% Southwest Airlines   78.10%   73.08%   0.85%   0.96% Allegiant Air   74.69%   72.59%   0.44%   0.73% Frontier Airlines   69.96%   70.21%   1.78%   2.15% JetBlue Airways   73.42%   67.74%   1.43%   4.08% Every airline listed canceled a larger share of flights than a year earlier. American ranks fourth for punctuality with an improvement of just 0.21 percentage points. Southwest and JetBlue each lost more than five points. United’s Premium Pitch Gets Ahead Of Its Operation United has improved its cabins, technology and network. I’ve argued that its broader schedule explains a lot of the customer preference Scott Kirby attributes to the brand. It’s a better airline than it used to be. Its operational results still don’t support treating it as anything close to an all-around leader. United blames the locations of its hubs, and says that it does well considering where it opreates. Its annual report points to hubs at the “most congested and constrained airports in the country.” It also benchmarks departures against competitors at its own hubs, rather than treating all airports as equally easy places to operate. In September, the category covering air traffic control, airport operations, traffic volume and ordinary weather accounted for delays on 8.57% of United’s flights, versus 5.78% at Delta. United also canceled a smaller percentage of flights than Delta or American through September, and it ranks third for on-time arrivals. But its punctuality declined and its cancellation rate rose from 1.34% to 1.75%. That’s nearly a 1/3 increase. And the weaknesses extend beyond on-time performance and completion factor. United ranks last for mishandled baggage. American was worst in full-year 2024, while United finished last in 2025. United remains last for the first nine months of 2026, and finished last separately in July, August and September. Here are mishandled bags per 1,000 checked bags, with a lower number being better. This includes delayed, damaged, lost and stolen bags. Airline network   Jan.–Sept. 2025   Jan.–Sept. 2026 Allegiant Air   0.9   1.3 Southwest Airlines   3.9   3.2 JetBlue Airways   3.1   3.4 Delta Air Lines   4.2   3.6 Alaska Airlines*   5.1   5.0 Frontier Airlines   3.8   5.2 American Airlines   6.8   6.6 United Airlines   7.4   6.9 United mishandles bags at nearly twice Delta’s rate. American remains last if you look only at the mainline airline: 7.2 per 1,000, versus United’s 6.6. United Express drags down United’s network result, while American Eagle improves American’s. Missed connections can cause bags to miss flights, too. So baggage problems aren’t entirely independent of congested hubs and delayed aircraft. Passengers buying connecting travel, though, have choices on which airline to connect and United doesn’t get a pass there because its hubs are less reliable. Then there are wheelchairs. United and Delta handled almost identical volumes: 105,534 at United and 105,559 at Delta. United mishandled 1,269. Delta mishandled 373. Delta Warned That Its Problems Would Last Through Summer. They Did. Back in May, I covered Delta’s cancellation problems and its executives’ warning that fixing them would take through the summer. Pilot availability, crew scheduling and recovery after disruptions were central problems. Chief Operating Officer Dan Janki said, “It’ll take us a little bit of time here as we work through it through the summer.” And Delta’s pilots didn’t actually go along with changes to contractual provisions that would boost reliability. They want something in return, and Delta hasn’t been willing to pay. Delta’s cancellation rate rose about 89%, from 1.19% to 2.25%. Subtracting the first-half figures from the latest report gives a third-quarter cancellation rate of 2.08%, versus 1.13% a year earlier. This is still a problem. Southwest’s Boarding Changes Had Costs That Were Easy To See Coming I warned before Southwest introduced checked bag fees that pushing luggage into the cabin would slow boarding and create more gate checking. Assigned seating then removed the incentive to board quickly to grab the best available seat, while making passengers hunt for bin space near a particular row. By March, flight attendants were pushing back over the consequences. Southwest was trying to get more flying out of its aircraft while making boarding less efficient. Through September, Southwest’s on-time arrival rate fell from 78.10% to 73.08%. Southwest handled 71.1 million checked bags, down from 84.7 million, while scheduling almost exactly the same number of domestic flights. That’s 16% fewer checked bag enplanements, now that they charge most passengers separately. People are now carrying their bags into the cabin instead of checking them as often. JetBlue’s Nice Onboard Product Can’t Make Up For Their Operation I’ve long described JetBlue as good in the air and a mess on the ground. Mint can be excellent. Even coach offers has been relatively pleasant, although JetBlue is enshittifying it in order to make room for domestic first class seating. But the operation lets down the product. The first nine months were bad: 67.74% on time and 4.08% canceled, both worst in the industry and their cancellation rate was nearly three times the same period last year. The summer was worse. Combining the July, August and September figures, only 61.85% of scheduled flights arrived on time during the third quarter. JetBlue canceled 6.28%, about one in sixteen flights. In July alone, it canceled nearly one in ten. September improved substantially, to 71.98% on time and 2.13% canceled. JetBlue still finished last on both measures that month. Actually getting a handle on this won’t fix JetBlue’s finances. They’re a baseline for a turnaround. Disruptions add expense, make repeat business harder to win, and undermine the value of the product the airline is spending money to improve. JetBlue needs customers to be able to buy its flight without budgeting for everything going wrong. Alaska Has Been A Perennial Leader Alaska leads the network on-time rankings at 78.64% and canceled 1.30% of its flights. That’s a better cancellation rate than any of the three largest network airlines. This is a longstanding strength. Back in 2015, I was asking why Alaska didn’t get more recognition for running such a strong operation when Delta received so much of the credit. Buying Hawaiian added an operation benefiting from the islands’ generally favorable weather. I pointed out that statistical advantage last year, and Hawaiian is now included in Alaska’s figures. But Alaska’s ability to run a good airline wasn’t something it bought with Honolulu. It was doing that long before the acquisition. American’s Bumping Numbers Are Finally Changing American involuntarily bumped 684 passengers in the third quarter, down from 4,318. That’s an 84% reduction, with almost unchanged passenger volume. Mainline American’s count fell nearly 90%, from 2,042 to 208. I broke the news of American’s new mandate against involuntary bumping. Airport managers can approve more compensation to find volunteers. Employees are supposed to keep the door open and take a delay if necessary. Volunteers can even be confirmed onto the very next departure when it’s already full. That directive took effect September 30. Nearly the entire quarter measured here came before it. The 84% decline shows the improvement that was already underway as American became more willing to pay volunteers. There’s another American improvement buried in the network totals. Comparing the third quarter with the same period last year: Mainline cancellation rate: improved from 2.21% to 1.46%. Regional partner cancellation rate: worsened from 2.44% to 3.17%. Combined network: almost unchanged, from 2.33% to 2.34%. American’s own flights became materially less likely to cancel over the summer, while American Eagle erased that improvement in the combined result. The bumping change also leaves Frontier looking particularly bad. It accounted for 69% of all involuntary bumps in the third-quarter table, despite carrying about 4% of the passengers. Delta secured 49,231 volunteers that quarter and involuntarily bumped nobody. Frontier recorded 841 volunteers and 2,514 involuntary bumps or roughly three unwilling passengers for every volunteer. The latest federal airline statistics show some results that don’t fit the usual reputations. It also shows why calling an airline “premium” requires more than nicer seats and better wifi. Strong operational performance isn’t enough but it’s the table stakes. An airline needs to get the basics right first, including delivering bags alongside their owners, as close to on-time as possible.

The Department of Transportation’s November Air Travel Consumer Report covers September and the first nine months of 2026. Here’s the domestic flight performance through September, and I take a look at how this performance compares to earlier trends.

Every airline listed canceled a larger share of flights than a year earlier. American ranks fourth for punctuality with an improvement of just 0.21 percentage points. Southwest and JetBlue each lost more than five points.

United has improved its cabins, technology and network. I’ve argued that its broader schedule explains a lot of the customer preference Scott Kirby attributes to the brand. It’s a better airline than it used to be. Its operational results still don’t support treating it as anything close to an all-around leader. United blames the locations of its hubs, and says that it does well considering where it opreates. Its annual report points to hubs at the “most congested and constrained airports in the country.” It also benchmarks departures against competitors at its own hubs, rather than treating all airports as equally easy places to operate. In September, the category covering air traffic control, airport operations, traffic volume and ordinary weather accounted for delays on 8.57% of United’s flights, versus 5.78% at Delta. United also canceled a smaller percentage of flights than Delta or American through September, and it ranks third for on-time arrivals. But its punctuality declined and its cancellation rate rose from 1.34% to 1.75%. That’s nearly a 1/3 increase. And the weaknesses extend beyond on-time performance and completion factor. United ranks last for mishandled baggage. American was worst in full-year 2024, while United finished last in 2025. United remains last for the first nine months of 2026, and finished last separately in July, August and September. Here are mishandled bags per 1,000 checked bags, with a lower number being better. This includes delayed, damaged, lost and stolen bags. Airline network   Jan.–Sept. 2025   Jan.–Sept. 2026 Allegiant Air   0.9   1.3 Southwest Airlines   3.9   3.2 JetBlue Airways   3.1   3.4 Delta Air Lines   4.2   3.6 Alaska Airlines*   5.1   5.0 Frontier Airlines   3.8   5.2 American Airlines   6.8   6.6 United Airlines   7.4   6.9 United mishandles bags at nearly twice Delta’s rate. American remains last if you look only at the mainline airline: 7.2 per 1,000, versus United’s 6.6. United Express drags down United’s network result, while American Eagle improves American’s. Missed connections can cause bags to miss flights, too. So baggage problems aren’t entirely independent of congested hubs and delayed aircraft. Passengers buying connecting travel, though, have choices on which airline to connect and United doesn’t get a pass there because its hubs are less reliable. Then there are wheelchairs. United and Delta handled almost identical volumes: 105,534 at United and 105,559 at Delta. United mishandled 1,269. Delta mishandled 373. Delta Warned That Its Problems Would Last Through Summer. They Did. Back in May, I covered Delta’s cancellation problems and its executives’ warning that fixing them would take through the summer. Pilot availability, crew scheduling and recovery after disruptions were central problems. Chief Operating Officer Dan Janki said, “It’ll take us a little bit of time here as we work through it through the summer.” And Delta’s pilots didn’t actually go along with changes to contractual provisions that would boost reliability. They want something in return, and Delta hasn’t been willing to pay. Delta’s cancellation rate rose about 89%, from 1.19% to 2.25%. Subtracting the first-half figures from the latest report gives a third-quarter cancellation rate of 2.08%, versus 1.13% a year earlier. This is still a problem. Southwest’s Boarding Changes Had Costs That Were Easy To See Coming I warned before Southwest introduced checked bag fees that pushing luggage into the cabin would slow boarding and create more gate checking. Assigned seating then removed the incentive to board quickly to grab the best available seat, while making passengers hunt for bin space near a particular row. By March, flight attendants were pushing back over the consequences. Southwest was trying to get more flying out of its aircraft while making boarding less efficient. Through September, Southwest’s on-time arrival rate fell from 78.10% to 73.08%. Southwest handled 71.1 million checked bags, down from 84.7 million, while scheduling almost exactly the same number of domestic flights. That’s 16% fewer checked bag enplanements, now that they charge most passengers separately. People are now carrying their bags into the cabin instead of checking them as often. JetBlue’s Nice Onboard Product Can’t Make Up For Their Operation I’ve long described JetBlue as good in the air and a mess on the ground. Mint can be excellent. Even coach offers has been relatively pleasant, although JetBlue is enshittifying it in order to make room for domestic first class seating. But the operation lets down the product. The first nine months were bad: 67.74% on time and 4.08% canceled, both worst in the industry and their cancellation rate was nearly three times the same period last year. The summer was worse. Combining the July, August and September figures, only 61.85% of scheduled flights arrived on time during the third quarter. JetBlue canceled 6.28%, about one in sixteen flights. In July alone, it canceled nearly one in ten. September improved substantially, to 71.98% on time and 2.13% canceled. JetBlue still finished last on both measures that month. Actually getting a handle on this won’t fix JetBlue’s finances. They’re a baseline for a turnaround. Disruptions add expense, make repeat business harder to win, and undermine the value of the product the airline is spending money to improve. JetBlue needs customers to be able to buy its flight without budgeting for everything going wrong. Alaska Has Been A Perennial Leader Alaska leads the network on-time rankings at 78.64% and canceled 1.30% of its flights. That’s a better cancellation rate than any of the three largest network airlines. This is a longstanding strength. Back in 2015, I was asking why Alaska didn’t get more recognition for running such a strong operation when Delta received so much of the credit. Buying Hawaiian added an operation benefiting from the islands’ generally favorable weather. I pointed out that statistical advantage last year, and Hawaiian is now included in Alaska’s figures. But Alaska’s ability to run a good airline wasn’t something it bought with Honolulu. It was doing that long before the acquisition. American’s Bumping Numbers Are Finally Changing American involuntarily bumped 684 passengers in the third quarter, down from 4,318. That’s an 84% reduction, with almost unchanged passenger volume. Mainline American’s count fell nearly 90%, from 2,042 to 208. I broke the news of American’s new mandate against involuntary bumping. Airport managers can approve more compensation to find volunteers. Employees are supposed to keep the door open and take a delay if necessary. Volunteers can even be confirmed onto the very next departure when it’s already full. That directive took effect September 30. Nearly the entire quarter measured here came before it. The 84% decline shows the improvement that was already underway as American became more willing to pay volunteers. There’s another American improvement buried in the network totals. Comparing the third quarter with the same period last year: Mainline cancellation rate: improved from 2.21% to 1.46%. Regional partner cancellation rate: worsened from 2.44% to 3.17%. Combined network: almost unchanged, from 2.33% to 2.34%. American’s own flights became materially less likely to cancel over the summer, while American Eagle erased that improvement in the combined result. The bumping change also leaves Frontier looking particularly bad. It accounted for 69% of all involuntary bumps in the third-quarter table, despite carrying about 4% of the passengers. Delta secured 49,231 volunteers that quarter and involuntarily bumped nobody. Frontier recorded 841 volunteers and 2,514 involuntary bumps or roughly three unwilling passengers for every volunteer. So if the issue with Delta is they signed a contract with the pilots that allowed this to happen — and may now have to give the pilots more to undo that — who at Delta was responsible for doing so (i.e., the screw up)?

Question: is the drop in baggage stats a reflection of United or the poor work ethic of employees. What I read here is it is a race to the bottom and none are considered “good”. Being the best or worse of this spiral is not a reason to brag.

In re: Alaska –> They don’t get much credit for their strong on-time performance and minimal cancellations because they remain something of a regional airline, focused primarily on the West Coast. So people in New York, Washington DC, Chicago, and other points east of the Rockies have less of an opportunity to fly Alaska compared with AA, DL, and UA. While Alaska “ain’t no Virgin America,” they remain — in my personal experience — heads and shoulders above the US Legacy Three. (Their 20-minute baggage guarantee certainly doesn’t hurt their reputation among passengers, either.)

Now comes the laughable story, what will be done to correct these problems? Charge more for bags, keep filling planes till 100% full and charge higher ticket prices for shorter routes.

LOL, just like schools need more to fix problems they created themselves.

Delta should get immediate credit for any cancellation of flights as it’s our nation and the worlds only true premium carrier Pinocchio with a growing nose

I’m glad you covered this data. It is the most impartial review of airline operational performance and it has been in existence for so long that there are easy trends to note.

First, regarding cancellations, DL’s cancellation problem early in the year was due to MAINLINE pilot scheduling. DOT data for August and Sept shows that DL’s mainline cancellation rate had returned to levels as good or better than AA and UA, all of which have large operations in the NE. DL did resolve its mainline pilot staffing issues in the first part of the 3rd quarter. The big 3 all have higher RJ cancellation rates because those flights are the first to be cancelled when weather forces extensive delays. LGA is by far the operationally worse large airport in the country and DL is the largest carrier. DCA used to be a pretty reliable airport but is not since the AA accident; if you remove all 3 NYC airports and DCA, cancellations with the big 3 are not that much different from other airlines including AS which has a very small presence in the delay prone NE.

as for on-time, as I noted in the other thread, AA is improving its operational performance and is very close to UA’s on-time in recent months. While DFW is prone to winter icing, winter is not kind to airports in the northern tier of the US so AA could overtake UA in on-time over the next few months.

AS gained its position with the best on-time as a result of the HA merger; HA had that title foryears. in Sept, DL overtook AS for the on-time lead with just a 0.3% gap between AS and DL in YTD on-time. It is very possible that DL could overtake AS. The real on-time story is how badly WN’s on-time has fallen; their execs said they are reluctant to add time to flights but their on-time is not improving. they have touted their win in the Wall Street Journal’s airline rankings but are unlikely to repeat precisely because their on-time is so low compared to the rest of the industry.

You are absolutely right that UA is stuck at the bottom of the industry in baggagehandling and don’t even acknowledge the problem, let alone do anything about it. Delta’s baggage handling is much closer to WN – which has a much less complex network than the legacies – than it is to AA or UA. It is also worth noting that AS might do well in on-time but it is mid-tier in most other statistics including baggage handling.

You didn’t cover complaint data which the DOT is now putting into the monthly report, although not with the ratios it once did. AA still gets way more complaints than any other airline with DL doing the best of the big 3 based on ratios while UA is just mid-tier. WN has a long history of resolving customer complaints at the point of contact and does well on complaint ratios. Frontier is where you will find the most complaints.

as much as some resist admitting it and will twist all kinds of statistics, DL is running the best operation of the big 4 on an overall basis. The WSJ’s best airline award is certainly not going to AA or UA

Delta threw $2500 at me (so, $7500 across three people counting the two at the gate) to get someone off the plane rather than do an IDB. They have their issues, but that is a real willingness to deal to avoid an IDB.

I hate to double post, but…squinting at that math, did DL VDB about 1 in 1000 pax? That seems a bit high, especially since it also feels like that means they had bumps on a significant portion of flights (and/or some massive oversales).

Delta also has the 20 minute baggage guarantee. But they simply cannot fulfill that for flights landing in Atlanta.

Every time I fly into Atlanta on Delta I get the 2500 pesos compensation for the bags being late. Not too late, probably around 25 minutes, which, by the time I get from the time door opens to the baggage corral, it’s only another 6-8 minutes wait.

Posted this question earlier at the bottom of another chain. Why is Allegiant’s mishandled baggage rate so high? Their model (point to point, almost no connections, no codeshare partners) should make it easy to board people’s bags on their flight.

Other observations, backed up by the latest data:

– We were right: Delta did have problems that lasted through the summer, as predicted by the many commenters (except one!) throughout the year and by Delta’s management themselves. The recent, “single month” stats in the latest report (September) are a month with reduced schedules and some of the best weather nationwide, so they should be viewed skeptically if anyone thinks they show any one airline’s problems are behind them. If issues remain (Delta’s pilot scheduling rules, American’s slow disruption-recovery, United’s congestion in ORD) they should show up again during the holidays.

– United is making headline-grabbing changes (best app features added / new routes / large plane orders / Starlink) but has lots of the basics to still improve upon. One of the big “we just opened it” stories was a new bag sorting facility in IAH, yet the needle hasn’t moved with improved mishandling as any consumer would want to see. They need to turn some attention to the basics.

– Alaska will now take the consistent lead in on-time performance and stats, as they will benefit from the former stat-leader (Hawaiian) and the fact that their merger partner operated flights at a hub that has perfect weather 98% of the time.

This is another reason why I don’t check bags, particularly on connecting flights.

Get the airline credit card, board early, and your bags fly in the cabin. Let the kettles deal with baggage claim.

no, Paul, DL HAD problems w/ mainline crew scheduling in the first half of the year. based on actual recent data, DL’s mainline cancellation rate is now BETTER than UA’s and their system on-time is the same.

IAH is such a small station in the scope of UA’s operation that it won’t move the needle in UA’s system baggage performance unless they were losing every other bag that went through IAH.

and DL DID beat AS in ontime performance in the most recent month – so your dream that DL will be the perpetual 2 has fallen apart.

As hard as it is for you to accept, when ALL data is reviewed, DL still runs the best operation of the big 4. DL still has to deal w/ the statistical weight that its winter 2026 crew scheduling issues had on its reliability but those are in the rearview mirror. unlike UA, DL has no category where it is consistently in the bottom tier – let alone consistently AT THE BOTTOM as UA is with baggage for almost 2 years straight.

LTD says, “DOT data for August and Sept shows that DL’s mainline cancellation rate had returned to levels as good or better than AA and UA”

No it doesn’t. Delta customers were 22% & 25% more likely to have their flights cancelled in July & August, respectively. Like PP said DL tied UA in September with good weather and therefore no recovery challenges. For the first nine months DL customers are 29% more likely to have their flight cancelled than UA. DL’s cancellation/recovery problem is back in November.

Tim Dunn bad analysis at work again. I”ll explain it like I would to a child.

1) September is an easy month. No stress on the system. Fewer flights, less disruptive weather.

2) Summer is harder. More flights, worse weather.

3) We are entering the holiday travel season (Thanksgiving, and going into Christmas). Winter weather is beginning to occur now. More flights are being added.

4) So, we will NOW be more like the SUMMER was, not like SEPTEMBER was.

Get it? That’s why year to date data means more than a single month. It better captures a period of operational history with conditions more similar to what we are going into, starting this week.

That’s also why Delta beating Alaska in one month doesn’t mean much. Don’t believe me about the affect of the summer? Look at Delta’s monthly stats. You can pick marketing carrier or mainline only. I don’t care. The trend is the same.

Delta On-Time July: 71.7% August: 77.0% September: 81.1%

See how it got better coming out of summer? You can believe the improvement is because Delta does things other airlines cannot. I believe it is weather and system saturation. The same trends are seen with other airlines:

July – August – Sept numbers: American: 68.8% –> 70.6% –> 72.5% Southwest: 68% –> 69.1% –> 72.8% United: 72% –> 71.1% –> 76.0%

See the general improvement? Rising tides raise all boats. Better weather and fewer flights are the tides and explain why Delta got better, along with everyone else. So when the winter weather returns and scheduled flights increase, you can expect to see these numbers (including Delta’s) trend back down. Simple analysis.

I’ll be happy to remind you about this again, when we get the monthly stats for December, early next year.

And before you jump on “Aha – United actually got worse in August than July!” you yourself said “a few percentage points” isn’t much difference. So a few TENTHS of a percentage shouldn’t be either.

Can’t wait to hear what I “just can’t stand to admit…” in reply.

In looking at the data you also need to note that Delta and JetBlue were affected by runway construction at Boston Logan which drove near daily ground stops for afternoon flights, Thankfully that is done, but I have come to love Flighty as a Boston based flyer.

son, I referenced the DOT data in the AA article long before Gary decided – of his own volition – to write an article directly about DOT data. As usual, you are incapable of getting the basic facts straight.

and Paul can’t grasp that the real operational story of 2026 for DL was DL’s pilot scheduling issues that really pushed DL’s mainline cancellation rates up. That problem has been dealt w/ by the end of the summer.

DL has long led the big 4 in on-time and that is still the case. All the fixation on 3 months of data and the stunning analysis that fall on-time is bettter doesn’t explain why UA hasn’t bested DL – or AS in on-time – but they haven’t.

It must be sad to be so incapable of admitting that someone else does something better than the airline that pays your salary that dodge and weave and obfuscate to avoid admitting that it is UA that blew the opportunity to overtake DL in operational reliability.

Now, DL is indeed generating cancellation rates as good or better than AA or UA and with better on-time. And DL loses bags at half the rate of UA, has virtualy no invol DBs despite having the highest vol DB rate (a story in and of itself) and has the complaint ratio of the big 3.

the beauty of DOT data is that it is so clear and yet some people work so hard to manipulate it.

When you're applying for a credit card, you may wonder: "How good is the welcome offer I'm applying for?"

There's no simple answer to this question, but knowing the previous offers a card has had can help you determine what constitutes a good welcome offer. Getting any welcome offer is better than getting nothing at all, but you wouldn't want to apply for a card only to see a better offer a month later.

Generally, you’ll want good to excellent credit to qualify for many of the Capital One cards on this list, though other factors can also affect your approval odds.

We’ve collected and analyzed the offer history over the past few years for Capital One's most popular cards and determined the best time to apply for each.

Limited-time offer on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Earn more than $1,000 in travel bonuses with a limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, plus earn 75,000 bonus miles once you spend $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

It's important to note that we'll only discuss publicly available welcome offers. However, you might receive targeted offers that offer more bonus miles or cash back. You can also check for preapproved Capital One offers without affecting your credit score, which may help you find targeted offers that are higher than the publicly available bonus.

Keep in mind that offers may change at any time, and some of those mentioned below may not be available.

The bonus offer values throughout this guide are based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and are not provided by the credit card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card earns an unlimited 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, plus 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, rental cars and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel.

The card’s modest $95 annual fee, simple earning structure and solid return on everyday spending make it a keeper once you’re approved for it.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture Rewards:

Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening (public offer).

The highest offer we've seen on this card allowed new cardholders to earn up to 100,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offers more than 75,000 miles — whether through additional miles or a travel credit — it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One Venture Business card is a straightforward option for business owners who want consistent travel rewards without having to track bonus categories. With a $95 annual fee, it offers simple earning rates, easy-to-use credits and flexible redemption options that help offset the cost year after year.

While it doesn’t come with premium perks like lounge access, its simplicity and solid earning structure make it a reliable long-term choice for everyday business spending.

The Venture Business's launch offer of up to 150,000 miles (75,000 miles after spending $7,500 on purchases in the first three months, plus an additional 75,000 miles after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months) is the best offer we've seen so far.

As a recently launched card, the Venture Business has only two bonus offers. Since there’s limited historical data, we recommend applying when the bonus is over 100,000 miles.

With plentiful, easy-to-understand perks, the Capital One Venture X is a no-brainer for all travelers, from luxury seekers to the more budget-minded, and the card practically pays for itself year after year.

Though the card carries a $395 annual fee, it offers a $300 annual credit toward bookings made through Capital One Travel and rewards cardholders with 10,000 bonus miles each account anniversary.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture X:

The highest offer we've seen on this card offered 100,000 bonus miles earned after spending $10,000 on purchases within the first six months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is 75,000 miles or higher, it's a good time to apply.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

The Venture X Business carries the same $395 annual fee as the personal version and offers the same major perks, including a $300 annual travel credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel and access to Capital One and participating Priority Pass lounges. It also carries the same earning rates as the Venture X.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Venture X Business:

The highest offer we've seen on this card is up to 400,000 bonus miles: Earn 200,000 miles after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, plus an additional 200,000 miles after spending $150,000 on purchases in the first six months.

When the bonus offer is for more than 150,000 miles, it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

While it comes with fewer perks, the Capital One VentureOne Rewards offers the same great redemption options as its sister cards, the Capital One Venture Rewards and the Capital One Venture X, with no annual fee. You’ll earn a flat 1.25 miles per dollar spent on everyday purchases.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One VentureOne Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen allowed new cardholders to earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 in the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offers more than 20,000 miles — whether through additional miles or a travel credit — it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card

The biggest downsides to cash-back cards are low earning rates and a lack of bonus categories, but that’s definitely not true of the Capital One Savor Cash Rewards.

For no annual fee, the Savor offers strong cash-back earning rates on popular and often overlooked categories, including 3% back on dining, entertainment and popular streaming services.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Savor Cash Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen included a $100 Capital One Travel credit to use in the first year. Plus, new cardholders could receive a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is $250 or more, it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards is another great card with no annual fee. It earns a reliable 1.5% cash back on all purchases, making it a perfect go-to card for the odd purchase that doesn’t fit in any bonus categories.

While many other cards offer higher earning potential in specific spending categories, this card offers the safety of knowing you’ll earn a solid 1.5% back no matter what you buy.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards:

The highest offer we've seen included a $100 Capital One Travel credit to use in the first year. Plus, new cardholders could receive a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

When the bonus offer is $200 or higher, it meets our criteria for applying.

Learn more: Capital One Quicksilver Cash Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One Spark Cash Plus earns 2% cash back on all purchases and is ideal for business owners who want to earn reliable cash-back rewards on all their expenses. It is worth noting that this is a no-preset-spending-limit card, meaning cardholders must pay off their balances in full each month.

The card has a modest $150 annual fee that can be refunded after spending at least $150,000 in your card anniversary year.

The highest welcome offer we've seen on this card offered up to $3,000: $500 after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening and $2,500 after spending $50,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening.

When the bonus is $2,000 or higher, it meets our application criteria.

The Capital One Spark Cash earns 5% cash back on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel and 2% cash back on all other purchases. With the flat rate earning structure, the card is ideal for businesses with spending across different categories.

The Spark Cash is a traditional credit card that allows cardholders to carry a balance, offering more flexibility for businesses that don’t want to pay their balance in full each month.

Here are the offers we've seen on the Capital One Spark Cash:

The highest welcome offer we've seen on this card is $1,500 in cash back after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

When the bonus exceeds $1,000, it meets our application threshold.

The Capital One Spark Cash Select is a solid option for small-business owners who want to earn straightforward cash-back rewards without paying an annual fee.

The card earns unlimited 1.5% cash back on all purchases, plus 5% cash back on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel.

The highest welcome offer we've seen on this card is $750 cash back after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

When the bonus exceeds $500, it meets our application threshold.
